Therefore, the woman wants to come to the hospital with the child to see a doctor to find out what can be done to help the child's body recover and be in a healthy state.
column19: The symptoms you describe—sudden crying with pain in the arms and legs, reluctance to move or bear weight—strongly suggest a condition like dactylitis, often the first painful crisis in sickle cell disease, which is common in our region. While awaiting your hospital visit, you can relieve the child's pain with age-appropriate paracetamol syrup (as per weight) and by applying warm compresses and gentle massage to the affected limbs. Ensure the baby stays well hydrated with frequent breastfeeding to reduce sickling and pain severity. At the hospital, the doctor will conduct a full evaluation, likely including a haemoglobin electrophoresis test, to confirm the cause and start early treatment to prevent developmental delays. Early diagnosis and proper management, including folic acid supplementation and pain control, will help your child recover and achieve healthy milestones.

column19: No, do not simply prescribe cough medicine and send them home. column18: ala bukun said that she has been having blurred vision together with weakness and that headache has not allowed her to be comfortable for about two weeks she has not been able to sleep well at night both her legs hands and face have been swollen she has been trying her best she was advised to take some things but she did not notice any improvement she was reassured that she would get better she was examined and there was no obvious respiratory distress all the important things that needed to be assessed were checked and there was nothing else significant she was able to climb its tair kiss without difficulty her blood pressure was checked and it was found to be 168 over 100 she was asked to rest and after some time with us her blood pressure was checked again and it was 150 over 90 it was noted that she was pregnant therefore treatment for high blood pressure that is suitable for pregnant women was started since it is considered safe in pregnancy she was also educated on all the things she should avoid doing especially avoiding excessive stress that could cause her blood pressure to rise further my question is after all the things that have been done for this kind of pregnant woman for pregnant women who have persistent headache and facial swelling what other measures can be used to manage such a pregnant woman without causing her condition to progress to convulsions considering that she is pregnant also what are the things a pregnant woman can do to prevent getting to this stage before she presents in such a condition
column19: To prevent convulsions (eclampsia) in this pregnant woman with severe features, she must be admitted for maternal and fetal monitoring and administered magnesium sulfate, which is the standard, evidence-based prophylactic anticonvulsant used locally. Finally, pregnant women should maintain a healthy lifestyle, avoid excessive stress, and immediately report danger signs like severe headaches, visual disturbances, or sudden swelling to a healthcare facility.

column18: Adeolu is a 10-year-old child whose mother was my sister. However, for a few days now, I have noticed that this child sits alone ever since his mother died. column19: Yes, Adeolu's withdrawal, loss of appetite, and reluctance to speak are classic signs of an acute grief reaction following the recent tragic loss of his mother. At this early stage, medication is not recommended, as experiencing deep sadness is a normal and necessary part of the bereavement process for a child. To help him at home, provide a patient, loving environment, gently offering small portions of his favorite foods without forcing him to eat, speak, or play before he feels ready. While he does not immediately need a psychiatrist for normal acute grief, connecting him with a child counselor or therapist can be highly beneficial to help him navigate and process his complex emotions. However, if his refusal to eat causes physical weakness or if this severe withdrawal persists for several weeks without improvement, he will need a professional pediatric mental health evaluation.

column18:
A mother noticed that for the past few days, her child had started coughing continuously. At first, she thought it was a cold affecting the child’s chest and that it would go away. However, the cough did not improve. Every night, the child wakes up suddenly because of the cough. Sometimes, the child struggles as if it is difficult to breathe properly. The mother would carry the child upright and could hear the chest working while the child was breathing. This makes it difficult for the child to sleep well at night.
One day, after a night during which the child coughed severely and struggled to breathe properly, the mother decided to go to the hospital. She wanted to know what was causing the cough, what was causing the breathing difficulty, and how she could help the child.
My question is: what could cause a child to cough severely and have difficulty breathing, especially at night? What danger signs should they watch out for when the child is coughing? What things should they avoid in order to prevent or reduce this cough?
column19:
A child experiencing severe coughing and difficulty breathing, especially at night, could be suffering from conditions such as asthma, pneumonia, or even a foreign body aspiration. Asthma is common in children and can cause nighttime symptoms due to allergens or viral infections. Pneumonia, which can be caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi, often presents with severe cough and breathing difficulties. Foreign body aspiration, though less common, can also cause these symptoms if a small object is inhaled. 

Danger signs to watch for include increased work of breathing, cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin, especially around the lips and fingertips), lethargy, and inability to feed. To help reduce the cough, ensure the child stays hydrated, avoid exposure to allergens, and use a humidifier. If symptoms persist or worsen, seek medical attention immediately. Avoid giving the child over-the-counter cough medicines without consulting a healthcare provider, as they may not be appropriate for children.

column18: a mother among the mothers who usually bring their babies for injections explained that she noticed that a newborn baby has a problem around the mouth and the baby's lips look bluish today she also noticed that when she is breathfeeding the baby the baby struggles gasps and finds it difficult to breath properly she said this is what made her worried because she does not know what is happening to the baby what can cause a newborn baby's lips to look blueys what can also cause a baby to struggle and have difficulty breathing while breathfeeding can medicine be given or should be baby be examined
column19: Bluish lips in a newborn indicate central cyanosis, a sign of dangerously low blood oxygen often caused by a congenital heart defect (such as Tetralogy of Fallot) or severe lung infection. Gasping and struggling during breastfeeding happens because the effort of feeding overwhelms the baby’s breathing; this can stem from heart failure flooding the lungs or from nasal blockage, since newborns breathe only through the nose. The combination strongly points to a serious heart or respiratory problem that needs urgent evaluation. Do not give any medication now—untargeted drugs, especially sedatives or cough syrups, may dangerously suppress breathing. Immediately take the baby to a hospital for a doctor to examine, measure oxygen levels, and provide life-saving care.

column18: A nursing mother noticed her child coughing and also suspected that the child's body was warm at certain times. column19: Mummy, the symptoms of coughing, stiffness, and foaming at the mouth indicate a very common condition called Cold-Induced Gastric Reflux, where chest congestion temporarily locks the child's nervous system. It is easily treatable, and your community's practice of using warm herbal mixtures and traditional soup is actually the best method to quickly relax those rigid muscles. column18: A guardian of a child observed that the child is cough intensely, till the end that the child is been abrupt and struggling to breathe well. column19: This presentation suggests severe respiratory distress possibly due to foreign body aspiration, severe bronchiolitis, croup, or status asthmaticus, requiring immediate assessment of airway patency and oxygen saturation. Urgent investigations include pulse oximetry, chest X-ray (inspiratory/expiratory views), and potentially bronchoscopy if foreign body aspiration is suspected. Treatment is etiology-specific: immediate removal of a foreign body via bronchoscopy, oxygen therapy, nebulized adrenaline and steroids for croup, or bronchodilators and systemic steroids for asthma. Ensure the child is positioned comfortably, avoid feeding if aspiration is suspected, and administer first-line antibiotics like amoxicillin if bacterial pneumonia is co-existing. Advise the guardian to seek emergency care immediately, avoid home remedies or forcing fluids, keep the child calm and upright, and ensure completion of prescribed medications and follow-up visits.

column18: a woman just gave bath to a newborn baby at our hospital this morning her delivery was very easy and she gave bet to the baby's motorly and without complications shortly after this woman gave baths we observed that the pad placed under her quickly became soaked with blood and it was quite a lot a few minutes later the woman used another pad yet it was also filled with blood very quickly before long the woman started feeling weak and the bleeding became so heavy that it did not stop what could be the cause of postpartum hemorrhage what could cause the bleeding to not stop is it possible that a second baby remains inside this woman is it possible that the woman's suffix is torn is it possible that a uterus is failing to contract to stop the bleeding what could cause the heavy continuous bleeding that this woman is experiencing what steps can we take for this woman to stop the bleeding what kind of injection or medication can be used for this woman and should we send this woman to a larger hospital or is there another procedure we can perform on this woman to make the bleeding stop
column19: This woman is experiencing primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), most likely due to uterine atony (failure of the uterus to contract), though a torn cervix from the rapid delivery or retained tissue like a second baby are also possible causes. Immediately perform uterine massage, establish two large-bore IV lines with crystalloid fluids, and administer uterotonic injections such as Oxytocin or Misoprostol to help the uterus contract. You must also perform a thorough vaginal examination to identify and repair any cervical tears, and palpate the abdomen to rule out a second undelivered baby. If the uterus remains boggy and bleeding continues, apply bimanual uterine compression as a temporizing measure while preparing for transfer. Because her weakness indicates severe blood loss, you must urgently refer her to a larger hospital for blood transfusion and advanced interventions like uterine balloon tamponade or surgery if the bleeding does not immediately stop.

What steps can we take for this woman to stop the bleeding? What kind of injection or medication can be used for this woman, and should we send this woman to a larger hospital, or is there another procedure we can perform on this woman to make the bleeding stop?
column19: The heavy continuous bleeding the woman is experiencing is likely due to postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), which can be caused by uterine atony (failure of the uterus to contract), retained placental fragments, or uterine rupture. Immediate steps to stop the bleeding include administering uterotonic drugs such as oxytocin, misoprostol, or ergometrine. If the bleeding does not stop with initial management, the woman should be transferred to a higher-level facility for further intervention, which may include surgical procedures like uterine artery embolization or hysterectomy. Close monitoring and supportive care are essential.

column19: The severe, increasing pain your daughter is experiencing is normal labor pain, which is caused by strong uterine contractions that help the cervix dilate (open) so the baby can be born. Please, we can give it to her again. Once she has finished eating and we have advised her to take paracetamol since she's feeling weak, if it doesn't go away, we will know what kind of treatment to provide.
column19:
Based on your description, this is a postpartum woman with fever (38.2°C), shivering, and a positive malaria rapid diagnostic test. Here is my guidance:

**Treatment of malaria:** For a breastfeeding mother, the recommended treatment is artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT), such as artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem), given as a full 3-day course. ACTs are safe during breastfeeding, so she can continue nursing her baby.

**Paracetamol:** Give 1000mg (two 500mg tablets) every 6–8 hours as needed for fever and pain, not exceeding 4g in 24 hours. She can safely repeat it every 6 hours, so no need to wait days between doses.

**Important warning — do not assume it is only malaria.** In a woman who delivered just hours ago, postpartum fever can also mean **puerperal sepsis** (uterine or genital tract infection). Please check her uterine tenderness, lochia (smell and amount), bleeding, blood pressure and pulse, and ensure she is passing urine.

**Action:** Start ACT plus paracetamol, encourage fluids and food, monitor her temperature and vitals closely, and if fever persists or she has foul-smelling lochia, uterine tenderness, or heavy bleeding, refer urgently for antibiotics and further evaluation.

column18: A woman had a baby—a child—about five months ago. She explained regarding the child that there was nothing wrong at the time she gave birth, as the baby was feeding vigorously as expected. column19: This child's presentation of acute limb pain, functional regression, and developmental delay five months post-delivery is highly concerning for **Vitamin D deficiency rickets with hypocalcemia**, **sickle cell disease (dactylitis/vaso-occlusive crisis)**, or **acute osteomyelitis/septic arthritis**. Early definitive diagnosis and treatment are critical to reverse bone deformities, relieve pain, and prevent permanent developmental delay.

column18: A 22 year old lady who gave birth at our hospital 3 days ago brought her baby today for routine immunizations. column19: This presentation is classic for severe neonatal sepsis, likely with hypothermia and probable hypoglycaemia; the “freezing cold” body is due to the baby’s inability to thermoregulate because of overwhelming infection, not simply from refusing the breast. The floppiness, lethargy, and absent reflexes indicate possible meningitis or septic shock, which demand immediate emergency management with warmth (skin-to-skin care or radiant warmer), intravenous antibiotics, and controlled dextrose fluids. Refusal to breastfeed is a symptom of this critical illness, so stabilizing the baby’s temperature, glucose, and infection is the first step—feeding can be given via nasogastric tube once stabilized. Do not administer any immunisations today; routine vaccines must be postponed until the baby is fully stable, active, and feeding well, typically after completing treatment and with a clear clinical improvement.

Does he need to visit a healthcare facility for testing, or is testing unnecessary? How often should diabetes screening or blood sugar testing be done, regularly or only occasionally? What medical conditions could be responsible for all these symptoms occurring in his body?
column19: These classic symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, blurred vision, fatigue, and weight changes strongly suggest uncontrolled Diabetes Mellitus, likely Type 2 given his age, though Diabetes Insipidus or renal pathology are differentials. He must visit a healthcare facility immediately for a fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, urinalysis (glucose/ketones), renal function tests (U&E), and lipid profile to confirm diagnosis and assess complications. He should adopt a calorie-controlled diet low in refined carbohydrates/sugars and high in fiber/vegetables, engage in regular moderate exercise (150 mins/week), avoid alcohol/smoking, and adhere strictly to prescribed medication if diagnosed. Diabetic screening should be done annually for high-risk adults (over 40, obese, family history) and 3-6 monthly for diagnosed patients to monitor control.

column18: a 30 year old woman gave bet a few minutes ago the delivery was said to be normal however since the baby was born the baby has been having serious difficulty the baby is not crying well and is not responding as a newborn should after bat the baby did not cry properly and seems to have difficulty waking up the body seems tiff or not moving properly as expected the baby also cannot feed well and is struggling to breathfeed the mother is worried because our previous children used to cry immediately after bat what can cause this problem what test can be done on the baby and what emergency steps should be taken what can be done for this newborn baby

column19: Beju's symptoms of chronic nocturnal cough and breathing difficulty since birth suggest a respiratory condition like infant asthma, reactive airway disease, or a chronic chest infection like tuberculosis, which can be effectively managed or cured once properly diagnosed at the hospital. column18: A grandmother noticed that her child, that she has been with after she gave birth, about three days ago, the bleeding following childbirth was heavier than normal. column19: The grandmother's child may be experiencing postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), a serious condition that can occur after childbirth. It is not caused by improper cleaning of the womb, but rather by various factors such as uterine atony, retained placental fragments, or coagulopathy. Immediate medical intervention is crucial, and treatments may include uterotonics, blood transfusions, and surgical interventions if necessary. The doctor will need to assess the situation thoroughly and provide appropriate care to stabilize the patient and prevent further complications.

column18: A caregiver who is taking care of a small child noticed that the child is caring for is struggling to breathe and the child's breathing is not normal. column19: A chest infection like pneumonia or bronchiolitis is the most common cause. Germs (viruses or bacteria) invade the lungs, causing inflammation and thick mucus that block the small airways. This makes it hard for air to flow in and out, so the child struggles to breathe and coughs severely to try to clear the blockage. These infections spread through droplets from coughs or contaminated hands, not from bathing with cold water. Take the child to a health facility immediately—they may need oxygen, antibiotics, or inhaled relievers—and keep the child sitting upright and calm during transport to help them breathe.

column18: A 30-year-old woman gave birth a few minutes ago. The delivery was said to be normal. However, since the baby was born, the baby has been having serious difficulty. The baby is not crying well and is not responding as a newborn should. After birth, the baby did not cry properly and seems to have difficulty waking up. The body seems Or not moving properly as expected. The baby also cannot feed well and is struggling to breastfeed. The mother is worried because her previous children used to cry immediately after birth. What can cause this problem? What tests can be done on the baby and what emergency steps should be taken? What can be done for this newborn baby?
column19:
# Likely Cause: Birth Asphyxia (Perinatal Hypoxia)

This presentation—poor cry, lethargy, weak tone, and poor feeding—most commonly indicates **birth asphyxia leading to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE)**. Other possibilities include **neonatal sepsis/meningitis, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, intracranial hemorrhage from birth trauma, congenital neurological conditions, or maternal drugs** given during labor.

## Emergency Steps (Immediate Resuscitation)
1. **Keep the baby warm** (dry, skin-to-skin or under a warmer) to prevent hypothermia.
2. **Follow the Helping Babies Breathe protocol**: position airway, suction if needed, and provide **bag-and-mask ventilation** with room air/oxygen if breathing is inadequate.
3. **Assess the APGAR score** and monitor heart rate, breathing, color, and tone continuously.

## Investigations
Check **blood glucose** (rule out hypoglycemia), **full blood count, blood culture, and CRP** (for sepsis), **serum electrolytes and calcium**, and a **blood gas** if available. Consider a **cranial ultrasound** and, where possible, **sepsis screen with lumbar puncture** if infection or meningitis is suspected.

## Management
Stabilize with warmth, oxygen, and correct hypoglycemia with **IV dextrose (10%)**. Start **IV antibiotics** empirically if sepsis is suspected, and give supportive care (IV fluids, monitor for seizures, treat with phenobarbitone if convulsing). **Refer urgently to a facility with neonatal care/incubator support** for close monitoring and further management.

column19: I’m going to think through the likely causes and the safest immediate steps, especially what should trigger urgent care.Severe lower abdominal pain in pregnancy with heavy bleeding can be caused by threatened miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental problems (like abruption or placenta previa), infection, fibroids, or preterm labor, and it needs urgent evaluation with examination and ultrasound. column19: Severe lower abdominal pain with heavy vaginal bleeding in pregnancy is an obstetric emergency most commonly caused by placental abruption, placenta previa, or uterine rupture, all of which pose immediate life-threatening risks to both mother and fetus. Heavy bleeding is a critical danger sign indicating potential hypovolemic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and fetal hypoxia or demise. Other warning signs include absent fetal movements, uterine tenderness or rigidity, signs of shock (tachycardia, hypotension), and preterm labor contractions. There is no safe outpatient medication to stop this bleeding or pain; definitive management requires immediate hospital admission for resuscitation, blood transfusion, and urgent delivery, often via cesarean section. She must present to a facility with surgical and blood banking capabilities immediately.

column18: A 33-year-old pregnant woman, who is 7 months pregnant, was brought to our hospital by her neighbors. They explained that she suddenly developed severe abdominal pain and a large amount of blood began to come out from her vagina. Her body was shaking and she was crying because the pain was intense. Her family said they were afraid that Something serious might happen to both the mother and the baby. Their first question for the doctor was, What could be causing this severe abdominal pain and hefy bleeding? Their second question was, What should be done immediately for this pregnant woman? Their third question was, What investigations or tests can be carried out? Their fourth question was, What treatment is appropriate for her condition? Their fifth question was what foods should this pregnant woman avoid and what hygiene measures should she observe?
column19:
The most likely cause is **placental abruption**—the placenta separates before delivery, causing **severe abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, uterine tightening/shaking and danger to mother and baby**; placenta praevia or uterine rupture are other emergencies to rule out.

She needs **immediate emergency care**: call obstetric/surgical team, put her on the left side, give oxygen, insert 2 large IV lines, start fluids, check vital signs and fetal heartbeat, take blood for urgent cross‐match, prepare blood transfusion, and do not allow her to eat/drink in case surgery is needed.

Tests include **full blood count, blood group/Rhesus and cross‐match, clotting profile, kidney function/electrolytes, bedside ultrasound for placenta and baby, urine test**, and continuous monitoring of bleeding, blood pressure, pulse and fetal heart rate.

Treatment is **resuscitation with IV fluids/blood, correction of clotting problems, anti‐D if she is Rhesus negative**, and usually **urgent delivery**—often Caesarean section if the baby is alive or mother is unstable, or induction/vaginal delivery if the baby has died and the mother is stable.

For now she should **avoid food/drink, alcohol, smoking, herbal drugs, sex, and inserting anything into the vagina**; maintain clean pads/perineal hygiene, wash hands, and after stabilization eat iron‐rich foods like beans, vegetables, meat/fish, and take prescribed iron/folate.

column19: Suberu, your persistent 3-month cough and worsening breathlessness most likely point to a chronic lung condition like pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), which is common in our environment, though asthma, chronic bronchitis, or even heart-related fluid buildup are also possible. Home remedies and over-the-counter cough syrups only soothe the throat or suppress symptoms temporarily but cannot cure an underlying infection or inflammation, so the disease continued to progress. To determine the exact cause, you need a chest X-ray and a sputum test (GeneXpert) to check for TB, plus a physical exam and possibly a lung function test. Once we have the diagnosis, we can start the correct treatment—such as a full course of anti-TB drugs, inhalers, or other targeted medications—which will clear the cough and help you breathe freely again. Please avoid further self-medication, as delaying proper care can lead to permanent lung damage or spread infection to your family.

column18: As a brave woman holding her child, seeing that the child is feverish, the child suddenly starts shaking. The child is having convulsions and is no longer in control. What kind of illness is affecting this nursing mother's child? And what kind of care can be given to this child?

Immediate first aid involves placing the child on their side in a safe position to keep the airway clear and preventing them from injuring themselves. You must never put anything in the child's mouth or try to restrain their movements during the shaking. Once the shaking stops, the child must be rushed to the nearest hospital immediately for intravenous fluids, anticonvulsants, and treatment of the underlying infection.

Because the wound is red and swollen, the doctor should clean/debride it, assess for pus or deep injury, give antibiotics such as **amoxicillin-clavulanate** for dog-bite infection, pain relief, and update **tetanus vaccination** ± tetanus immunoglobulin depending on immunization history.
Tests are not usually needed for rabies prevention, but if the wound is deep, very swollen, has pus, or is near a joint/bone, the hospital may do wound culture, blood tests, or X-ray, and the dog should be observed for 10 days—but the child’s rabies treatment should not be delayed.

column18: a mother of a young child became worried about her eight month old baby during the daytime the baby plays well but every night the baby starts coughing the cough wakes the baby from sleep and the baby cries afterwards on one of those nights the mother noticed that the baby was breathing very fast and seemed to be struggling to breathe the mother could not sleep because of fear the following morning she noticed that the baby did not want to breast feed uply as before so she decided to take the baby to see a doctor because she wanted to know what was causing the cough and the breathing difficulty and to know what medicine or treatment could be used for the baby my question is what could cause a young child to cough severally at night and also make it difficult for the child to breathe properly could the cough and the struggle to breathe properly be signs of a long disease what are the things that can be done at home to help the baby become more comfortable and sleep better at night
column19: The severe nighttime cough, fast breathing, and poor feeding strongly indicate an underlying lung disease such as acute bronchiolitis, early childhood asthma, or pneumonia. At night, mucus pools in the respiratory tract and the airways naturally narrow, which worsens the breathing struggle and triggers severe coughing in an infant with inflamed lungs. Because fast breathing and a sudden refusal to breastfeed are critical "danger signs" of severe respiratory distress in our local guidelines, taking the baby to the clinic was the right step to get urgent treatments like oxygen, nebulization, or antibiotics. To help the baby be more comfortable at home, ensure the room is well-ventilated and strictly avoid exposing the child to lung irritants like cooking firewood smoke, cigarettes, or mosquito coils. Additionally, you can slightly elevate the baby's head during sleep to ease breathing, use normal saline drops to clear a blocked nose, and offer breast milk frequently in small amounts to maintain hydration.

column18:
​A 22-year-old lady who gave birth at our hospital three days ago brought her baby today for routine immunizations. Upon arrival, she made it known to us that this newborn baby completely refuses to breastfeed at all, to the extent that the baby is excessively floppy and sleepy. She stated that the baby does not take the breast, and that all the time, the baby's hands, feet, and entire body feel freezing cold, so much so that she is even terrified to touch the baby with bare hands and prefers to lift the baby only with layers of clothing. She noted that the baby refuses the breast, the entire body is cold to the touch, and the baby has become increasingly lethargic,unable to move the hands, unable to stretch the legs, and completely lacking active movement or reflexes, just lying completely still and weak. She says it is obvious to the eye that the baby is exhausted and very unwell.
​What could cause this? What do you think could cause this newborn baby's body to be freezing cold to the touch? Is it solely because of the refusal to breastfeed, or what else? What can we do about this refusal to breastfeed? Furthermore, regarding the immunization vaccines they are supposed to administer, what is your professional advice?
column19: This neonate presents with severe hypothermia, profound hypotonia, absent reflexes, and feeding refusal, which collectively indicate life-threatening neonatal sepsis, possible meningitis, or severe metabolic derangement (e.g., hypoglycemia, inborn error of metabolism), rather than simple starvation. The "freezing cold" temperature results from the baby's inability to thermoregulate due to energy depletion, hypothalamic immaturity, and the underlying severe illness causing peripheral vasoconstriction and shock. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate admission to a Special Care Baby Unit for warming (kangaroo mother care or incubator), rapid IV access for 10% dextrose bolus and maintenance fluids, empiric IV antibiotics (Ampicillin plus Gentamicin or Cefotaxime per local protocol), and urgent investigations (RBS, CBC, blood culture, lumbar puncture if stable). Do not administer any routine immunizations today; the baby is critically ill and vaccines are contraindicated in acute severe illness—defer until full recovery. Prioritize stabilization and referral to a higher-level facility if ventilatory or advanced neonatal support is unavailable.

column18: doctor a mother living in our house began to notice that her baby was not breastfeeding well whenever she tried to breastfeed the baby the baby would suck for a little while and then stop as if exhausted the mother also noticed that the baby did not have enough strength for breastfeed and would sweat heavily on the head and face not only that the baby's breathing changed it seemed as though the baby was breathing upward and downward like someone struggling to breathe as the days went by the mother became increasingly worried she wondered whether it was because the baby was not feeding enough or whether there was a problem related to the baby's breathing and sweating therefore she decided to go to the hospital to see a doctor for an examination of the baby my question is what could cause a baby to have difficulty breastfeeding properly is the way the baby is breathing a sign of any health problem what danger signs should the baby's parents watch out for what could cause a young child to sweat while breastfeeding
column19: The baby's difficulty breastfeeding, exhaustion, and heavy head sweating are classic signs of congestive heart failure, typically caused by congenital heart disease, where the physical effort of sucking acts like heavy exercise for a failing heart. The abnormal, labored breathing is a major danger sign of respiratory distress, which could be driven by heart failure or a severe respiratory infection like pneumonia, both of which are common in our environment. Other locally relevant causes for these combined symptoms include severe anemia, possibly from malaria or sickle cell disease, and severe sepsis. Parents should urgently watch out for danger signs such as bluish discoloration of the lips and tongue (cyanosis), severe chest in-drawing, grunting noises, extreme limpness, and refusal to feed. The mother was absolutely right to go to the hospital, as this is a medical emergency requiring immediate clinical evaluation, oxygen support, and diagnostic tests like an echocardiogram to save the baby's life.

column18: My name is Mrs Akinleye. For about the past two months, I have noticed that my husband's breathing has not been normal at all. He also sneezes repeatedly, especially whenever he is in a dusty environment or in a place where something is being fried. He sneezes repeatedly and finds it difficult to breathe properly. His breathing becomes labored and he tends to sneeze whenever he's in places with smoke. Smoke or dust, is there any test that can be carried out to determine exactly what is causing these symptoms? Could staying in dusty places be the cause or is his body's system changing in a way that is making this happen? What type of medication can he use so that his breathing will become normal and comfortable at all times wherever he may be?
column19: Welcome, Mrs. Akinleye; your husband's symptoms strongly suggest a combination of allergic rhinitis and allergic asthma, where his immune system is overreacting to environmental irritants. To determine the exact cause, we can perform a lung function test called spirometry to assess his airway, alongside allergy tests (like a skin prick test) to identify specific triggers. It is a combination of both factors you mentioned: the dust and smoke act as environmental triggers, but his body's heightened allergic sensitivity is the underlying cause of the reactions. To normalize his breathing, he will likely require antihistamine tablets to control the sneezing, as well as prescription inhalers—a daily preventer inhaler to reduce inflammation and a fast-acting reliever inhaler like Salbutamol for emergencies. Please bring him to the clinic for a proper physical examination so we can confirm this diagnosis and prescribe the appropriate medications for his specific needs.

column18:
Good evening doctor. Please, I brought my child to the hospital because I noticed that the way he breathes, he makes a sound as if air is passing through a small hole. It sounds like wheezing. It also sounds like someone blowing a whistle, and he is struggling to breathe properly.
I have also noticed that for about three days now, he usually coughs at night. Sometimes, I notice his chest drawing in and out intensely, as if he is working extra hard just to breathe. I also noticed that he can no longer eat well as before. Whenever he wants to eat, he has to pause to catch his breath. This situation hasn't given him the chance to feed properly for about three days now.
I have already taken him to the local chemists (patent medicine stores) in our neighborhood, and they gave me some cough medicine for him because he was coughing slightly, though the cough wasn't severe. But despite all the medication he took, I noticed it didn't work. His breathing remains the same, and he still cannot eat well. Please, what kind of condition is affecting my child with this whistling breath? Also, does he need a chest examination (X-ray) to find out what is troubling him and why his chest is heaving up and down? What kind of treatment can I give this child at home to help ease his breathing so he can breathe properly? Are there other medications or alternative measures I can take for this child?
column19: The child may have a condition called asthma, which causes difficulty in breathing and wheezing. A chest examination and possibly an X-ray are necessary to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other conditions. At home, you can use a cool-mist humidifier to help ease breathing and ensure the child stays hydrated. Inhalers with bronchodilators or corticosteroids may be prescribed by a doctor to manage symptoms. It's important to follow the doctor's advice and keep the child away from known asthma triggers.

column18: As a brave woman holding her child, seeing that the child is feverish, the child suddenly starts shaking. The child is having convulsions and is no longer in control. What kind of illness is affecting this nursing mother child, and what kind of care can be given to this child?
column19:
The child is likely experiencing a **febrile convulsion**, which is a seizure triggered by a rapid rise in body temperature (fever).

During the seizure, immediately place the child on their side (recovery position) on a flat, safe surface to protect their airway, loosen any tight clothing, and do not put anything in their mouth or restrain their movements. Once the shaking stops, gently sponge the child's body with lukewarm (tepid) water to help lower the fever, avoiding cold water or methylated spirit.

Finally, once the child is fully conscious, you can administer paracetamol to help manage the fever, and immediately take them to the nearest healthcare facility to identify and treat the underlying cause of the fever, such as malaria or a bacterial infection.

column18: suddenly we saw one of our pregnant women who came to our hospital this morning she arrived in severe pain crying loudly holding her back an abdomen because of the pain after about eight to ten minutes of bringing her into the labour world we examined her and found that the baby was already descending and her service was fully dilated very shortly afterward she delivered a baby girl so we carried out all the necessary and appropriate post delivery care not long after we moved the mother and baby into a room so they could rest a little while later the mother called us and said she was feeling very weak tired and that her eyes seemed dim or blurry she also tried to eat after delivery but struggled to do so and the food was not going down well she continued to feel weak and she was also feeling dizzy what could have her food could it be that she lost a lot of blood and now she needs a blood transfusion or what should be done for her should we give her blood or should we give her food
column19: The combination of blurred vision, dizziness, profound weakness, and difficulty swallowing shortly after a rapid delivery suggests either significant postpartum hemorrhage (causing anemia and hypovolemia) or postpartum pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (visual disturbances, epigastric pressure mimicking dysphagia). Immediately assess her vital signs, check uterine tone and lochia for excessive bleeding, and evaluate for pallor, tachycardia, or high blood pressure. If she is bleeding heavily with signs of shock, urgently cross-match and transfuse blood; if her blood pressure is severely elevated with visual changes, treat as severe pre-eclampsia with magnesium sulphate and antihypertensives. Do not give food or drink until she is stable and can swallow safely, as forcing food in a dizzy, weak patient with impaired swallowing risks aspiration. Base your intervention on clinical findings—blood transfusion for hemorrhage, medical management for hypertension—and only resume oral intake when she is alert, normotensive, and free of dysphagia.

column18: a 22 year old lady who gave birth at our hospital three days ago brought a baby today for routine immunizations upon arrival she made it known to us that this newborn baby completely refused to breastfeed at all to the extent that the baby is excessively floppy and sleepy she stated that the baby does not take the breast and that all the time the baby's hand feet and entire body feel freezingly cold so much so that she is even terrified to touch the baby with bare hands and prefers to lift the baby only with layers of clothing she noted that the baby refuses the breast the entire body is called to the touch and the baby has become increasingly lethargic unable to move the hands unable to stretch the legs and completely lacking active movements or reflexes just lying completely still and weak she says it is obvious to the eye that the baby is exhausted and very unwell what could cause this what do you think could cause this newborn baby body to be freezing cold to the torch is this only because of the refusal to breastfeed or what else what can we do about this refusal to breastfeed furthermore regarding the immunization vaccines that they are supposed to administer what is your professional advice
column19: This baby is experiencing a life-threatening medical emergency likely caused by severe neonatal sepsis leading to dangerous hypothermia (freezing cold body) and severe hypoglycemia, which goes far beyond a simple refusal to breastfeed. The extreme floppiness and inability to feed are late signs of systemic infection and metabolic collapse; therefore, you must immediately stop oral breastfeeding attempts to prevent aspiration. Quickly admit the baby for urgent resuscitation, provide immediate thermal care using a radiant warmer or incubator, and commence intravenous (IV) dextrose to correct the blood sugar alongside empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. In our environment, neonates lack the energy reserves to fight infections and regulate body temperature simultaneously, making immediate sepsis screening and stabilization critical to saving this child's life. Furthermore, you must absolutely defer the routine immunizations (BCG, OPV, and Hepatitis B) until the baby is fully treated and clinically stable, as administering vaccines to an acutely ill, unstable neonate is contraindicated and unsafe.

column18: a 33-year-old pregnant woman who is several months pregnant was brought to our hospital by our neighbors the explained that she suddenly developed sevia abdomina pain and a large amount of blood began to come out from avajaina our body was shaking and she was crying because the pain was intense our family said they were afraid that something serious might happen to both the mother and the baby their first question for the doctor was what could be causing this severe abdominal pain and healthy bleeding their second question was what should be done immediately for this pregnant woman their third question was what investigations or tests can be carried out their fourth question was what treatment is appropriate for a condition their fifth question was what food should this pregnant woman avoid and what idean methods should she observe
column19: The sudden severe abdominal pain and heavy vaginal bleeding in this stage of pregnancy strongly point to placental abruption, a life-threatening emergency where the placenta prematurely detaches from the womb. Immediately, she must be resuscitated with fast-flowing intravenous (IV) fluids and oxygen to stabilize her blood pressure and prevent severe hemorrhagic shock. We must urgently carry out an obstetric ultrasound scan to check the baby's heartbeat and the placenta's position, alongside a full blood count, blood grouping, and cross-matching to prepare for a necessary blood transfusion. The definitive treatment is prompt delivery, typically through an emergency Cesarean section, to control the bleeding and give both the mother and baby the best chance of survival. During recovery, she should avoid alcohol, undercooked meats, and unwashed raw foods, while maintaining strict perineal hygiene by washing from front to back with clean water and changing sanitary pads frequently to prevent infections.

column18: A mother peju who has three children, peju is the junior child. Peju is a one-year-old child. Peju's mother noticed that, just a few days after childbirth, Peju has had a cough illness and has been coughing continuously without stopping at all. She said she also noticed that it is difficult for her to breathe well. She said this cough appears mostly in the evening, when everyone has gone to sleep. She said her breath is also difficult to breathe well, because this cough does not allow her to breathe in and out properly. What are the things that the child needs to avoid so that this problem affecting her and causing her to cough can be significantly reduced?
column19: Peju's symptoms, including persistent cough, difficulty breathing, and worsening at night, are concerning and could indicate a respiratory condition such as asthma or a chest infection. Given the ineffectiveness of the harbor mixtures, it is important to seek further medical evaluation. The child should avoid exposure to potential allergens, irritants, and respiratory infections. Ensuring good indoor air quality, avoiding tobacco smoke, and maintaining good hygiene practices are essential. A thorough examination, including a chest X-ray and possibly spirometry, will help in diagnosing the exact cause and determining the appropriate treatment.

column18: my husband is 40 years old and i suddenly notice that for about the past three weeks he has been drinking water excessively the more water he drinks the more frequently he urinates in fact at night he may wake up as many as 10 times before money just to urinate he has also complained of feeling tired all the time he has gained a little weight as well sometimes his vision becomes bloody and he says he does not see clearly when he gets up to move around i have noticed that he passes your rain in large amounts and very frequently what could be causing this frequent urination and excessive test what does it seem to drink so much why does it seem to drink so much water and then urinate so often could these symptoms be signs of diabetes or could they indicate something else what type of medical test should he undergo to determine exactly what is happening why is he constantly tired what causes the frequent urination could eyeblood pressure cause these symptoms or could they be due to dehydration or another condition what kind of foods and drinks should he avoid and what should he be encouraged to consume what steps should he take to help these symptoms improve does he need to visit a healthcare facility for testing or is testing unnecessary how often should diabetes screening or blood sugar testing be done regularly or occasionally what medical conditions could be responsible for all these symptoms occurring in his body
column19: Your husband’s symptoms of excessive thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurry vision strongly point to Diabetes Mellitus, a condition where high blood sugar forces the kidneys to excrete excess glucose and water, leading to severe dehydration and cellular energy depletion. While high blood pressure can coexist, these specific symptoms are directly driven by this metabolic imbalance rather than hypertension or simple dehydration alone. He needs to visit a healthcare facility immediately for diagnostic tests, including a Fasting Blood Glucose (FBG), HbA1c, and a urinalysis to check for glucose and ketones. For now, he must strictly avoid sugary drinks, sodas, and refined carbohydrates, opting instead for plenty of water, vegetables, and fiber-rich local foods like unripe plantain or oats. While regular diabetes screening is recommended annually for adults over 40, his current severe symptoms require urgent, immediate medical attention rather than routine screening.

column18:
After I gave birth and I was trying to recover, one evening I thought that since we did not have clean water in our area, if I wanted to bathe, I would always use water that is not clean all the time, I kept thinking that I should take care of myself and be bathing properly.
Then, when it became one evening, my body was no longer well. I started feeling cold, and my body began to shiver every day. I was feeling cold, but my body was not well again. I noticed that the blood that was coming out after childbirth had a smell coming from there that was not good at all. The smell was much, and this had not happened before.
I could not take my eyes away from it. As I got up, that was when I was coming to the hospital to ask whether the clean water that I used to bathe could cause any illness after childbirth
column19: Your symptoms of fever, rigors, and foul-smelling lochia strongly suggest puerperal sepsis, a serious postpartum uterine infection requiring urgent medical evaluation. This condition is caused by bacterial ascent into the genital tract during or after delivery, not by bathing with unclean water, though poor hygiene can increase risk. You need immediate assessment including vital signs, pelvic examination, and likely blood cultures, urine microscopy, and a high vaginal swab. Treatment involves prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (typically covering anaerobes, gram-negatives, and gram-positives) and possible evacuation of retained products of conception if ultrasound suggests it. Please present to the hospital immediately for admission and management to prevent progression to septic shock.

column18:
A mother noticed that for the past few days, her child had started coughing continuously. At first, she thought it was a cold affecting the child’s chest and that it would go away. However, the cough did not improve. Every night, the child wakes up suddenly because of the cough. Sometimes, the child struggles as if it is difficult to breathe properly. The mother would carry the child upright and could hear the chest working while the child was breathing. This makes it difficult for the child to sleep well at night.
One day, after a night during which the child coughed severely and struggled to breathe properly, the mother decided to go to the hospital. She wanted to know what was causing the cough, what was causing the breathing difficulty, and how she could help the child.
My question is: what could cause a child to cough severely and have difficulty breathing, especially at night? What danger signs should they watch out for when the child is coughing? What things should they avoid in order to prevent or reduce this cough?
column19: A child coughing severely and having difficulty breathing, especially at night, could be due to several causes such as asthma, pneumonia, bronchitis, or even a foreign body aspiration. Danger signs to watch for include persistent fever, bluish lips or face, lethargy, inability to eat or drink, and worsening symptoms despite treatment. To help reduce the cough, ensure the child stays hydrated, avoid exposure to allergens or irritants, and follow prescribed medications. If symptoms persist or worsen, seek medical attention immediately. Avoid giving the child over-the-counter cough medicines without consulting a healthcare provider, as they may not be appropriate for children.

column18: I took my pregnant friend who is 18 years old to the hospital because she had gone into labor and her time had come. When we arrived at the hospital and they had carried out all the necessary assessments, her blood pressure was high. After they had completed all that needed to be done, she continued in labor. She remained in labor for about 12 hours. Her husband was nearby and the doctors advised that she should give consent for a Kesarian section. because she had been in labor for a long time. My friend refused. She said, No, not at all. I want to give birth naturally like the Hebrew woman. She eventually delivered the baby. After 12 hours of labor, she gave birth to a healthy looking baby girl and we thanked God. However, what was surprising was that the baby was not breathing properly. They stimulated the baby repeatedly, patting and rubbing her. She cried, but her breathing was still not normal. They quickly gave her oxygen. Doctor, please, will this baby survive? And if she survives, will she now become a disabled child?
column19: We thank God for the safe delivery, and you can rest assured that the baby will survive perfectly without any form of disability. The breathing difficulty is simply because the baby was tired from the long labor and swallowed some amniotic fluid, which the oxygen mask will easily dry up. Since the nurses patted her and made her cry, her lungs are now fully expanded, meaning her brain has escaped any danger. Furthermore, your friend's high blood pressure actually helped the situation by pumping extra oxygenated blood into the baby's head, completely protecting her nervous system from damage. Once she finishes taking the oxygen, just keep her very warm and she will grow up to be completely normal like every other child.

column18:
Good evening doctor. Please, I brought my child to the hospital because I noticed that the way he breathes, he makes a sound as if air is passing through a small hole. It sounds like wheezing. It also sounds like someone blowing a whistle, and he is struggling to breathe properly.
I have also noticed that for about three days now, he usually coughs at night. Sometimes, I notice his chest drawing in and out intensely, as if he is working extra hard just to breathe. I also noticed that he can no longer eat well as before. Whenever he wants to eat, he has to pause to catch his breath. This situation hasn't given him the chance to feed properly for about three days now.
I have already taken him to the local chemists (patent medicine stores) in our neighborhood, and they gave me some cough medicine for him because he was coughing slightly, though the cough wasn't severe. But despite all the medication he took, I noticed it didn't work. His breathing remains the same, and he still cannot eat well. Please, what kind of condition is affecting my child with this whistling breath? Also, does he need a chest examination (X-ray) to find out what is troubling him and why his chest is heaving up and down? What kind of treatment can I give this child at home to help ease his breathing so he can breathe properly? Are there other medications or alternative measures I can take for this child?
column19: The symptoms you describe, including wheezing, nocturnal coughing, and difficulty breathing, suggest that your child may have asthma. Asthma is a common chronic condition characterized by inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to breathing difficulties. An x-ray of the chest can help rule out other conditions, but it is not always necessary for asthma diagnosis. For home treatment, you can use a short-acting bronchodilator (rescue inhaler) to help ease breathing. Additionally, ensure your child stays away from known asthma triggers, such as allergens and irritants. If symptoms persist or worsen, seek medical attention for further evaluation and management.

column18: i am 32 years old i just gave bet i just gave bet seven days ago i noticed that if i am breastfeeding the child he struggles to soak the breast if the child soak a little bit the child will remove his mouth if i try to put the breast in his mouth so he can soak he will soak again a little bit and remove his mouth i now thought that why did the child doesn't soak breast well i now noticed that the child has cold is not breathing out well like a child snoring that's how he sounds i call the attention of my mother-in-law she say maybe while we want to give birth to the child maybe water enters his head or other things but i thought if water enters his head the nurses and doctors ought to know if water enters the child's head what now shattered my heart the most was the way he's not feeding well it given me concern and my mind is not at rest he doesn't suck well at all it's by force any time i want to breastfeed the child i have to wake him to suck a little that's if he agrees to what i want to ask is that what's the cause of the cold that he doesn't breathe well and that any time he breathed it would look like someone that the nose is blocked and that what is the cause that he's not sucking breast well
column19: Your baby’s difficulty feeding is very likely because his nose is blocked. Newborns breathe only through their noses, and even a small amount of mucus or amniotic fluid can cause the snoring sound and make him pull away from the breast to gasp for air. This is common in the first week and is not a sign that “water entered his head”; your birth team would have detected any serious problems. Before each feed, try clearing his nose with a couple of saline drops and a soft bulb suction, and keep his head slightly raised while breastfeeding. However, if he becomes too weak to wake, breathes very fast, develops a fever, or his lips look blue, take him to the hospital immediately as these could signal a serious infection.

column18: A newborn baby that has just been delivered in our hospital for about 20 minutes ago was found to appear sleepy. The baby did not cry well since being delivered. When we checked its respiration it was fine but the baby was asleep all through. We also checked the temperature and it was normal. Here is my question. What could cause a newborn baby to appear as if it is sleeping and not cry properly since its birth. Also what kind of treatment? Will be effective for such baby and when the mother gets home, what could she administer to the child and what she should not and what kind of food should the mother eat to ensure that both the mother and baby will be healthy.
column19: The baby is just suffering from normal birth fatigue from the stress of delivery, which naturally makes them sleep deeply without crying much. For immediate treatment in the ward, you should drop a little pure honey on the baby's tongue to give it instant energy and clear the throat. When they get home, she can give the baby some warm water with a few drops of *agbo ọmọ* (infant herbal mixture) to keep the baby active, but she must not breastfeed until her real white milk starts flowing. She must strictly avoid giving the baby that first yellowish milk (colostrum) because it is too stale and heavy for a newborn's weak stomach. To ensure good health, the mother should eat very hot, spicy pepper soup to pass warming energy through her breastmilk, while avoiding drinking too much water so her milk doesn't become weak and watery.

column18: A woman was brought to the hospital this morning because she was bleeding heavily and this had caused her a great deal of distress. She was asked whether this had happened to her before and she replied that it had happened about twice previously, during which she usually experienced pain and the bleeding would occur intermittently. She was then asked whether she might be having a miscarriage, but she said she did not know whether she was pregnant. or whether she had become pregnant. She was asked when she last had her menstrual period and she replied that it had not been very long as she had her last menstrual period about one and a half months ago before this bleeding started again this morning. Please, what could cause a woman to bleed this heavily? What emergency steps can be taken? What treatment can be given to this woman to save her life and stop the bleeding? What may Medicines or injections that help stop bleeding can be given to her first and what investigations can be carried out to determine the cause of such severe bleeding.
column19:
The heavy bleeding, pain, and delayed menses us hence suggest pregnancy-related complications like an incomplete miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or molar pregnancy, though uterine fibroids or dysfunctional uterine bleeding are also possible.

Immediate emergency steps require securing two large-bore IV lines to infuse crystalloids (like Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate) for resuscitation, while closely monitoring her vital signs.

To stop the bleeding, uterotonics such as oxytocin, misoprostol, or ergometrine can be administered, and a manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) may be performed if retained products of conception are confirmed.

Urgent blood transfusion should be initiated if she is hemodynamically unstable or severely anemic.

Finally, critical investigations include a urine pregnancy test, a pelvic ultrasound, a complete blood count, and blood grouping with cross-matching.

column18:
A woman who lives in our house, she is employed. She does her work diligently and has no health issues.
One day, while she was bathing, she felt her breast and noticed something like a small, hard lump inside it.
Initially, she thought it was nothing serious, but she felt it again on another day and realized it was still there. As time went on, she became very anxious. She began to worry about whether this issue was developing within her breast. It wasn't painful, but the fact that the lump was hard and wouldn't go away made her sad. She also started remembering stories she used to hear about girls who had lumps in their breasts.
After a few weeks, she decided to go see a doctor. She wanted to know what caused the lump and what she needed to do to safeguard her health.
My questions are: What can cause a hard lump in a woman's breast?
Does every breast lump mean something that could lead to cancer?
What other symptoms should women look out for regarding their breasts?
column19: A hard breast lump can be caused by several conditions, including benign ones like fibroadenomas (common in younger women), cysts, infections (mastitis), or malignant tumors like breast cancer. Not every lump is cancer; in many cases, they are non-cancerous, but any persistent, hard, or fixed lump must be clinically evaluated to rule out malignancy. Women should also watch for warning signs such as skin dimpling (peau d'orange), nipple discharge, nipple retraction, persistent redness, or significant changes in breast size or shape. In our clinical practice, the standard next step is a physical examination followed by an ultrasound or mammogram and potentially a fine-needle aspiration (FNA) to confirm the diagnosis. Early detection is key, so she should see a doctor immediately for a formal diagnostic workup to alleviate her anxiety.

column18: I sent my son to buy a wedding for me in the neighborhood yesterday evening. After about 15 minutes, he suddenly came home crying. When I asked what had happened, they told me that a dog had bitten him on the leg. I asked what kind of dog it was and where it came from, but they said they didn't know where the dog came from or whether it was a neighborhood dog. At that point, I applied oil to the place where the dog bit him. To neutralize the poisoning of the dog. Afterwards, I was advised to take him to a maternity clinic in the neighborhood. I took him there and they prescribed a tetanus injection for me to buy from a chemist. I bought the injection and it was administered to him yesterday. I have since taken him home but since yesterday, the wound has become swollen and the surrounding area is red. I am now worried that the dog may have transmitted rabies to my child. I would like to ask whether Whether there is any medicine I can buy for him or whether I should take him to a hospital for further treatment.
column19: You must take your son to a general hospital immediately instead of buying medicines from a chemist, as the wound's redness and swelling indicate a secondary bacterial infection requiring prescription antibiotics. Because the dog is unknown and rabies is highly endemic in Nigeria, your child urgently needs a full course of anti-rabies vaccines (Post-Exposure Prophylaxis) which must be properly scheduled and administered by medical professionals. Applying oil to a bite wound is a harmful practice that traps bacteria, whereas the correct first aid is to wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes to reduce the viral load. While the tetanus injection was a good step, please proceed to the hospital's emergency unit right now to initiate the life-saving rabies vaccine schedule and treat the current wound infection.

When I asked what had happened, they told me that a dog had bitten him on the leg.
