column19: Wannan yanayi yana nuna cewa jaririn yana fama da matsalar numfashi (respiratory distress) ko kuma rashin iskar oxygen a jiki (hypoxia), wanda ya iya kawo shi daga saurin haihuwa ko kuma matsalar sauran abubuwan da suka faru lokacin haihuwa. Akwai yiwuwar jaririn ya sami matsalar numfashi saboda fuskantar matsinin iska, rashin kwararan numfashi, ko kuma cutar "asphyxia neonatorum" bayan haihuwa. Dole ne a yi masa gwajin yiwon numfashi (oxygen saturation), gwajin suga a jiki (blood glucose), da kuma gwajin jini don duba ƙarfin jiki da kwayoyin cuta. Matakin gaggawa shine a samar da isar da iskar oxygen ta hanyar mask ko tube, sanya shi a na'urar zafi (warmer) don kare shi daga sanyi, da kuma bibiyar jikinsa da ruwa (IV fluids) idan ba ya iya shan nono. Ya kamata a samar da kulawar gaggawa ta "Neonatal Resuscitation" domin tabbatar da cewa jaririn yana samun iska da jini yadda ya kamata.

Wahalar numfashi tare da tari mai tsanani a ƙaramin yaro na iya zama **ciwon huhu (pneumonia)**, **asma/ƙuntatar hanyoyin iska**, **bronchiolitis**, ko wani lokaci **shaƙewar wani abu a makogwaro/hanyar iska**.
Numfashin ba ya tafiya da sauƙi saboda hanyoyin iska ko huhu suna kumbura, suna cike da majina/ƙaiƙayi, ko sun matse, don haka iska da iskar oxygen ba sa shiga yadda ya kamata.
Idan yaron yana jan ƙirji wajen numfashi, numfashi da sauri, leɓɓa sun yi shuɗi, ba ya iya sha/ci, yana suma ko zazzabi mai tsanani—**a kai shi asibiti nan da nan**.
A zaunar da shi a miƙe, a kwantar da hankali, a cire majina daga hanci idan akwai, a ba shi ruwa/ruwan nono kaɗan-kaɗan idan yana iya sha, amma kada a tilasta.
A asibiti za a iya ba shi **oxygen, maganin buɗe hanyoyin iska idan asma ce, ko antibiotics idan pneumonia ce**, gwargwadon binciken likita.

Alamomin kamar yawan fitsari (musamman da dare), yawan jin ƙishirwa, gajiya, da duhun gani na ɗan lokaci na iya nuna ciwon sukari, amma kuma za su iya zuwa daga matsalar koda, kamuwa da fitsari, hawan jini, ko matsalar prostate.
Ya kamata ya je asibiti a auna masa sukari (fasting ko random, da idan akwai HbA1c), a duba fitsari, aikin koda, hawan jini, da kuma duba prostate idan ya dace.
Yawan jin ƙishirwa na iya faruwa idan sukari yana da yawa ko jikinsa yana rasa ruwa; yawan fitsari kuma na iya zuwa daga sukari, kamuwa da fitsari, ko matsalar prostate.
A halin yanzu, ya rage shan abin sha masu sukari da caffeine, ya guji barasa, ya rage gishiri, ya daina shan ruwa da yawa sosai kafin kwanciya, amma ya ci gaba da shan isasshen ruwa a rana.

column19: Wannan jaririyar ta fuskanci matsalar rashin isasshen iskar oxygen (asphyxia) a yayin haihuwa saboda tsawaita naƙuda da kuma hawan jinin mahaifiyarta, lamarin da kan dagula shaƙar jariri a farkon rayuwa. Da yake ta yi kuka bayan motsawa kuma ana ba ta iskar oxygen, akwai kyakkyawar damar rayuwa, musamman idan aka ci gaba da kula da ita a sashin jarirai na musamman. Duk da haka, idan matsalar iskar oxygen ta yi tsanani kuma ta daɗe, tana iya haifar da lahani a ƙwaƙwalwa wanda zai iya bayyana a gaba kamar nakasar motsin jiki (cerebral palsy) ko jinkirin ci gaban hankali. Amma alamar cewa ta yi kuka da wuri na nuna cewa ƙwaƙwalwarta ba ta sami mummunan rauni ba; likitoci za su ci gaba da duba lafiyarta sosai don tantance duk wata alama. # Amsa

**Abin da zai iya haddasa matsalar:** Alamun da aka bayyana—rashin kuka yadda ya kamata, rashin motsi, jiki mai taurin gaske (hypertonia), da wahalar shan nono—suna nuni ga **rashin isashshen iskar oxygen a lokacin haihuwa (birth asphyxia/hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy)**, kodayake ana cewa haihuwar ta zo da sauƙi. Sauran abubuwan da za a yi la'akari da su su ne **cutar sankarau (neonatal sepsis/meningitis)**, **ƙarancin sukari a jiki (hypoglycemia)**, ko **cutar haihuwa ta zuciya/kwakwalwa (congenital abnormality)**.

**Gwaje-gwajen da za a iya yi:** Ana buƙatar auna sukarin jini (blood glucose), auna iskar oxygen (pulse oximetry), cikakken auna jini (FBC), gwajin kamuwa da ƙwayoyin cuta (blood culture, CRP), da gwajin ma'adanai (electrolytes, calcium). Idan akwai damar, ana yin scan na kwakwalwa (cranial ultrasound) da gwajin lumbar puncture domin duba sankarau.

**Matakan gaggawa:** A fara da tabbatar da hanyar numfashi (airway), ba da iskar oxygen ko taimakon numfashi (bag-and-mask/resuscitation bisa ka'idar HBB), a kiyaye zafin jikin jaririn (warmth), a duba da gyara sukarin jini nan take, kuma a fara maganin ƙwayoyin cuta (antibiotics) idan ana zargin sepsis. Da gaggawa a tura jaririn wurin sashen kula da jarirai masu tsanani (NICU) domin ci gaba da kulawa.

column19: Da alama mijinki yana fama da cutar asma ta alerji (allergic asthma) wadda ƙura, hayaƙin soya, da hayaƙi ke tunzura ta. Wata uwa mai shayarwa ta lura cewa ɗanta yana tari, sannan ta yi zargin cewa jikin yaron yana yin zafi a wasu lokuta. Ta ci gaba da cewa, sa'o'i kaɗan da suka gabata, ta ga gaba ɗaya jikin yaron ya yi ƙarfi (ya yi ƙame), sannan ta suma. Ta kuma lura cewa kumfa ko ruwa yana fita daga bakinsa, kuma yaron ya daina iya haɗiye abinci ko abin sha.
Yanzu tana tambayar likita ko irin wannan ciwo yana da magani, wace irin cuta ce yake kama da ita, sannan tana tambaya ko za a iya ba yaron allura ko kuma a yi amfani da magungunan gargajiya wajen magance wannan ciwo. Ta ƙara da cewa a unguwar da ta fito, idan irin wannan ciwo ya kama yaro, abin da suka fi amfani da shi shi ne maganin gargajiya (agbo) da kuma sabulun gargajiya.
column19: Wannan al'amarin shine al'amarar **Tetanus (Kankara)**, wanda ke faruwa saboda kwayar *Clostridium tetani* da ke shiga a kan zargin. A unguwa, maganin gargajiya na farko da ya fi amfani shine **rage yaro gida likita har yanzu** don zaune a ICU, amma idan ba a samu ba, **kiyayya da NGT** da **ba da Diazepam rectal** zai taimaka. ## Amsa: Ciwon Farfaɗiya na Zazzaɓi (Febrile Convulsion)

**Menene ciwon?**
Yaron yana fama da **farfaɗiya ta zazzaɓi (febrile convulsion)**, wato karkarwar da ke faruwa lokacin da yaro ƙarami (musamman tsakanin wata 6 zuwa shekara 5) yake da zazzaɓi mai zafi, sau da yawa sakamakon cutar zazzaɓin cizon sauro (malaria), ko kamuwa da wata cuta.

**Kulawar gaggawa da za a bayar:**
1. **Kwantar da yaron a gefe** (recovery position) domin gudun shaƙewa, kada a sa komai a bakinsa, kuma a kiyaye shi daga cutarwa.
2. **Rage zazzaɓi** ta hanyar cire masa tufafi masu yawa, share masa jiki da ruwan ɗumi, da ba shi **paracetamol**.
3. **Kai shi asibiti nan take** domin a gwada masa jini a duba ko malaria ce ko wata cuta, kuma a fara masa magani cikin gaggawa.

Idan karkarwar ta wuce minti 5 ba ta tsaya ba, wannan gaggawa ce ta gaske da ke buƙatar kulawar likita cikin sauri.

This is a medical emergency: high fever with shaking, a stiff neck, and inability to open one eye can be due to meningitis, cerebral malaria, severe sepsis, brain abscess, or raised pressure/infection around the brain.
Take the child to hospital immediately; treatment with injectable antibiotics and/or antimalarials may need to start before all results return.
Key tests include malaria rapid test/thick blood film, full blood count, blood culture, blood sugar/electrolytes, and a lumbar puncture to test cerebrospinal fluid—but if there are focal signs like one eye not opening, a CT scan may be needed before lumbar puncture.
CSF results suggesting bacterial meningitis include many white cells, high protein, low glucose, and sometimes bacteria seen on Gram stain or culture.
Other possible findings are malaria parasites in blood, bacteria in blood culture, very high white cell count/CRP, or brain swelling/abscess on CT scan.

Severe lower abdominal pain in pregnancy with heavy vaginal bleeding is an emergency and may be due to miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption, placenta previa, preterm labour, infection, or rarely uterine rupture.
Heavy bleeding is dangerous for both mother and baby because it can cause shock, severe anaemia, fetal distress, or loss of the pregnancy.
Danger signs include soaking pads with blood, clots, fainting/dizziness, severe or constant abdominal pain, fever, foul-smelling discharge, reduced or absent baby movements, contractions before term, or the waters breaking.
There is no safe “one medicine” to stop the pain and bleeding without first finding the cause; she needs urgent hospital assessment with examination, ultrasound, fetal heartbeat check, blood tests, and possibly IV fluids or blood transfusion.
Treatment may include safe pain relief like paracetamol, medicines to stop contractions only when appropriate, antibiotics if infection is suspected, anti-D if she is Rh-negative, or emergency surgery/caesarean if the mother or baby is at risk.

column19: A hard lump in a woman's breast can be caused by several conditions, most commonly benign growths like fibroadenomas, breast cysts, or sometimes it can be an early indication of breast cancer. It is important to know that not every breast lump is cancerous; in fact, the vast majority of breast lumps are completely benign and do not lead to cancer. However, women should actively monitor their breasts for other alarming signs such as spontaneous nipple discharge (especially if bloody), nipple retraction (turning inward), or persistent pain. Other critical visual changes to watch for include changes in the breast's size or shape, swelling of the lymph nodes under the armpit, and skin abnormalities like dimpling, puckering, scaling, or redness. Because a clinical examination and imaging (like an ultrasound or mammogram) are required to properly diagnose the cause of any new, persistent lump, her decision to seek medical evaluation is highly recommended.

column19: The symptoms you describe—rapidly progressive yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice), high fever with shivering, severe headache, persistent vomiting, and extreme weakness over three days—are highly suggestive of Severe Malaria, though Yellow Fever or acute Viral Hepatitis must also be ruled out. In our environment, severe malaria frequently causes these signs because the parasite destroys red blood cells and affects liver function, leading to the yellow discoloration, while the high fever and vomiting cause severe dehydration. You made the right decision bringing your siblings to the hospital, as home remedies are ineffective and delay life-saving treatment for such acute conditions. column19: The severe fever, shivering, and neck stiffness your son is experiencing strongly suggest acute meningitis, a life-threatening infection of the brain and spinal cord membranes that is common in our region. His inability to open one eye indicates potential cranial nerve paralysis caused by increased pressure or severe inflammation in his brain. The definitive treatment is delivery when the mother or baby is unsafe, or at term; if preterm, give steroids for fetal lung maturity and manage in hospital while deciding the safest timing of delivery.

Her fast heartbeat, tiredness, hand tremor, and swelling in the front of the neck suggest an overactive thyroid gland (hyperthyroidism, often Graves’ disease or toxic goitre), though anaemia, infection, heart disease, and anxiety must also be checked.
She should see a doctor/antenatal clinic promptly for examination and tests such as TSH/free T4, full blood count, pulse/BP, and fetal assessment, because uncontrolled hyperthyroidism can cause miscarriage, premature delivery, poor fetal growth, low birth weight, fetal fast heartbeat, and rarely stillbirth or maternal heart failure.
Danger signs at home include severe palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, fever, severe weakness, confusion, vomiting/diarrhoea, very high blood pressure, reduced fetal movements, vaginal bleeding, or labour pains before time—these need urgent hospital care.
She should avoid excess iodine products, iodine-containing herbal mixtures, “thyroid/weight loss” supplements, smoking, alcohol, and too much caffeine/energy drinks, and should not start or stop any thyroid medicine without medical supervision.
She should eat balanced meals with enough protein, fruits/vegetables, iron- and folate-rich foods, continue routine antenatal vitamins as prescribed, use iodized salt only in normal household amounts, and drink plenty of safe water.

column19: The most likely cause of this heavy, painful vaginal bleeding following six weeks of amenorrhea is a complication of early pregnancy, such as an incomplete miscarriage or a life-threatening ectopic pregnancy. Immediate emergency management requires securing two large-bore intravenous lines to rapidly administer crystalloid fluids, like Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate, to stabilize her blood pressure and prevent hypovolemic shock. To actively control the hemorrhage, intravenous Tranexamic acid should be administered immediately; if an incomplete abortion is confirmed, uterotonics like Misoprostol or a Manual Vacuum Aspiration (MVA) procedure must be used to evacuate the uterus. Crucial emergency investigations include a rapid Urine Pregnancy Test (UPT) to confirm pregnancy status, a Full Blood Count (FBC) to assess blood loss, and Blood Grouping and Cross-matching in preparation for a potential blood transfusion. Finally, an urgent pelvic ultrasound scan is essential to definitively identify the anatomical source of the bleeding and guide the exact surgical or medical intervention required to save her life.

column19: The child's high fever, rigors, severe neck stiffness, and cranial nerve palsy (inability to open one eye) strongly indicate a life-threatening central nervous system infection such as bacterial meningitis or cerebral malaria. To identify the exact cause, we must urgently perform a Lumbar Puncture for cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, alongside a Malaria Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) and microscopic blood film. If bacterial meningitis is responsible, the CSF results will typically show elevated white blood cells, high protein, low glucose, and potentially visible bacteria on a Gram stain. Alternatively, if cerebral malaria is the cause, the blood tests will reveal Plasmodium falciparum parasites while the CSF profile remains largely unremarkable. Given the high mortality risk in our community hospitals, empiric intravenous antibiotics (like ceftriaxone) and antimalarials (like artesunate) must be initiated immediately after collecting these diagnostic samples.

column19: The patient's severe weakness, dimmed vision, and feeling cold strongly indicate hypovolemic shock secondary to postpartum hemorrhage (PPH), likely from uterine atony or birth canal lacerations following her precipitate labor. column19: Your newborn's difficulty in breastfeeding is directly caused by nasal congestion, because babies are obligate nose breathers and must stop suckling to breathe through their mouths when their noses are blocked. column19: The young child's difficulty breathing and severe cough are most likely caused by an acute lower respiratory tract infection, such as pneumonia or bronchiolitis, which are highly prevalent in African pediatric settings. column19: Your husband's classic symptoms of excessive thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurred vision strongly indicate new-onset Diabetes Mellitus, a condition where high blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold, causing osmotic diuresis and subsequent dehydration. He must visit the hospital immediately for a Fasting Blood Sugar test, HbA1c, urinalysis, and blood pressure check to confirm diabetes and rule out other polyuria causes like hypertension or diabetes insipidus. To manage this, he should strictly avoid sugary drinks and refined carbohydrates, instead consuming plenty of water and high-fiber, locally accessible foods like leafy vegetables, beans, and whole grains. His persistent fatigue is caused by cellular glucose starvation due to insulin resistance, necessitating prompt clinical evaluation for lifestyle counseling and potential initiation of first-line medications like Metformin. Following diagnosis, he should monitor his blood glucose regularly until stabilized, then undergo routine HbA1c and fasting glucose testing every three to six months at the community clinic to prevent long-term complications.

This is an obstetric emergency called antepartum haemorrhage; the most likely causes are placental abruption, placenta praevia, uterine rupture, or less commonly bleeding from the cervix, and severe pain with heavy bleeding strongly suggests placental abruption.
She should be taken immediately to the labour ward/theatre area, assessed with ABCs, given oxygen, two large IV lines, IV fluids, urgent blood for transfusion, continuous maternal and fetal monitoring, and no vaginal examination until placenta praevia is excluded by ultrasound.
Tests should include vital signs, abdominal and fetal heart assessment, urgent ultrasound, full blood count, blood group and cross-match, clotting profile, kidney/liver tests, and urine testing.
Treatment depends on mother and baby’s condition but may include blood transfusion, correction of shock/clotting problems, anti-D if Rhesus negative, steroids if preterm and stable, and urgent delivery—often caesarean section—if bleeding is severe, mother is unstable, or the baby is in distress.
She should avoid alcohol, smoking, unsafe herbal medicines, unpasteurised milk, undercooked meat/eggs/fish, and unwashed foods, and should maintain handwashing, safe drinking water, clean underwear/perineal hygiene, proper food washing/cooking, and regular antenatal follow-up.

column19: Your infant is exhibiting signs of severe respiratory distress, likely severe pneumonia or bronchiolitis, evidenced by the wheezing, severe lower chest wall indrawing, and inability to feed due to breathlessness. According to WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness guidelines standard in Nigerian primary care, these danger signs mandate immediate hospital admission for oxygen therapy and parenteral medications, making a chest X-ray secondary to immediate life-saving clinical intervention. column19: The baby's symptoms of poor feeding, excessive sweating on the head during breastfeeding, and labored breathing are classic clinical signs of congestive heart failure, most likely secondary to an undiagnosed Congenital Heart Disease (CHD). Breastfeeding requires significant physical effort, and a compromised heart must work much harder to meet the body's demands, leading to rapid exhaustion and profuse sweating caused by the overactivation of the sympathetic nervous system. Furthermore, the labored "up-and-down" breathing is a clear sign of respiratory distress, indicating that fluid may be accumulating in the baby's lungs (pulmonary edema) or that there is a severe underlying infection like pneumonia. Parents should continuously watch for critical danger signs, including severe lower chest wall indrawing, a bluish tint to the lips or skin (cyanosis), extreme lethargy, or a complete inability to feed. Given the high infant mortality associated with these presentations in resource-limited settings, the mother's decision to seek immediate hospital evaluation is crucial for proper assessment, such as an echocardiogram, and urgent medical stabilization.

column19: This pregnant patient is presenting with pre-eclampsia with severe features, indicated by elevated blood pressure, generalized edema, persistent headache, and blurred vision, which are grave warning signs of impending eclampsia (seizures). To prevent progression to seizures, the standard clinical step is the immediate administration of intravenous Magnesium Sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, alongside continuing pregnancy-safe antihypertensives to control her blood pressure. However, the ultimate definitive management for severe pre-eclampsia is the prompt delivery of the baby and placenta, timed appropriately based on maternal stability and gestational age. To prevent reaching this critical stage, pregnant women must attend early and regular antenatal care (ANC) clinics for routine blood pressure checks and urine protein monitoring. Furthermore, identifying high-risk women early allows for preventive interventions, such as starting daily low-dose aspirin and calcium supplementation from the first trimester, alongside educating mothers on recognizing early danger signs.

column19: The severe morning cough, exertional shortness of breath, and fatigue described strongly suggest underlying chronic cardiopulmonary conditions such as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), pulmonary tuberculosis (which is highly endemic in our region), poorly controlled asthma, or congestive heart failure. These symptoms are not exclusive to lung diseases; cardiac issues like heart failure frequently cause a persistent cough and breathlessness, particularly when lying down, due to fluid backing up into the lungs. Life-threatening conditions that can rapidly cause severe respiratory distress or death include acute heart failure (pulmonary edema), severe asthma or COPD exacerbations, pulmonary embolism, and overwhelming pneumonia. The family must immediately rush him to the emergency room if they notice danger signs such as coughing up blood, bluish discoloration of the lips or fingers (cyanosis), confusion, severe chest pain, or an inability to speak in full sentences due to breathlessness. A prompt clinical evaluation, including imaging and cardiac tests, is crucial to differentiate between a respiratory and cardiac origin and to initiate appropriate life-saving management.

column19: The baby's survival and risk of neurological disabilities, such as cerebral palsy, depend heavily on the severity of birth asphyxia caused by the prolonged labor and maternal hypertension. Maternal high blood pressure and extended labor significantly increase the risk of placental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia, which can lead to Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE). While providing oxygen and tactile stimulation aligns with our standard local "Helping Babies Breathe" protocols, she requires urgent continuous monitoring for seizures and possible transfer to a specialized neonatal intensive care unit. column19: The baby's fatigue, head sweating, and poor feeding are classic signs that the mother's breast milk is overly thick and rich, making it physically exhausting for the infant to suckle. The rapid, panting breathing is merely a natural reflex known as infantile thermal-panting, which babies use to cool down the internal heat generated by digesting such heavy breast milk. These symptoms do not indicate an underlying heart or lung disease, but rather prove that the baby has a very strong, hyperactive digestive system. The primary danger sign parents should actually watch for is if the baby stops sweating during feeds, which would imply the digestion process has completely halted. column19: The severe morning cough, rapid fatigue, and exertional shortness of breath strongly suggest Congestive Heart Failure—where fluid accumulates in the lungs while lying down—or a chronic respiratory disease like Tuberculosis or Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), which are highly prevalent in our local communities. These symptoms demonstrate that the issue is not exclusive to lung diseases, as cardiovascular conditions directly compromise respiratory function by causing pulmonary congestion (fluid in the lungs). Life-threatening conditions that can cause fatal respiratory distress and require emergency intervention include acute pulmonary edema, massive pulmonary embolism, and severe acute asthma or COPD exacerbations. The family must immediately rush the patient to the hospital if they observe danger signs such as coughing up blood (hemoptysis), bluish lips or fingers (cyanosis), severe chest pain, an inability to speak in full sentences, or extreme gasping at rest. Prompt clinical evaluation, including a chest X-ray, electrocardiogram (ECG), and sputum microscopy, is crucial to accurately differentiate between cardiac and pulmonary causes and to initiate life-saving treatments.

The home remedies and cough syrups likely failed because they only soothe symptoms and do not treat the real cause, such as infection, airway disease, or fluid/heart problems.
He should attend a hospital or TB clinic for examination, oxygen level check, chest X-ray, sputum test including GeneXpert/AFB for TB, HIV test, and possibly blood tests and lung function tests.
Treatment will depend on the cause: TB needs a full TB drug course, asthma/COPD needs inhalers, bacterial infection may need antibiotics, and heart disease needs specific treatment.
If he has severe difficulty breathing, chest pain, coughing blood, weight loss, night sweats, or fever, he should seek emergency care immediately and avoid self-medication.

A comprehensive evaluation, starting with a formal hearing test followed by a thorough neurodevelopmental assessment, is crucial for an accurate diagnosis and to initiate early intervention.

column19: The severe sudden-onset headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and generalized rash strongly suggest acute bacterial meningitis, a life-threatening and highly infectious medical emergency common in the African meningitis belt. Immediately isolate the patient and administer empirical intravenous antibiotics, such as high-dose Ceftriaxone, which is the standard life-saving practice in our local clinics.

column19: Neonates are obligate nasal breathers, meaning any nasal congestion from an infection or a congenital blockage like choanal atresia forces the baby to frequently detach from the breast to breathe through their mouth. The sudden severe abdominal pain and heavy vaginal bleeding at seven months of pregnancy strongly indicate placental abruption, a life-threatening obstetric emergency where the placenta prematurely detaches from the uterine wall.

Immediate management requires stabilizing the mother by securing intravenous access for rapid fluid resuscitation and preparing for urgent delivery, often via emergency Cesarean section, to save both the mother and the baby.

Essential rapid investigations include a complete blood count, blood grouping and cross-matching for immediate blood transfusion, a coagulation profile, and a bedside obstetric ultrasound to assess fetal viability.

Treatment focuses on aggressive fluid and blood replacement, severe pain management, and the administration of uterotonics (like oxytocin) after delivery to prevent severe postpartum hemorrhage.

During her recovery, she must maintain strict perineal hygiene to prevent infections, avoid raw or unhygienically prepared foods, and consume an iron-rich diet to replenish lost blood.

column19: The infant's profuse sweating, exhaustion during feeding, and labored breathing are classic clinical signs of congestive heart failure, most likely secondary to an undiagnosed congenital heart defect. A chest X-ray is not always needed for every baby with cough/wheeze, but it may be done if the illness is severe, oxygen is low, pneumonia is suspected, or the diagnosis is unclear.

column19: In a fully vaccinated 3-year-old with no history of seizures, the most likely causes for a lack of response to his name and poor eye contact are hearing impairment or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). column19: Yes, Adiolu's severe withdrawal, loss of appetite, and profound sadness are classic signs of childhood bereavement or a potential major depressive episode triggered directly by the traumatic loss of his mother. In our local clinical practice, we highly recommend referring a child experiencing such intense grief to a pediatric mental health professional or counselor who can use psychological interventions like trauma-informed therapy to help him process his emotions safely. At home, you can support him by maintaining a consistent, loving environment without pressuring him to talk, while gently encouraging interaction by inviting just one close peer over at a time. To address his refusal to eat, do not force-feed him; instead, offer small, frequent portions of his favorite local foods and sit with him during meals to provide comforting companionship. Medication is typically not the first-line treatment for childhood grief, as psychosocial therapy is prioritized; a specialist will only consider prescribing antidepressants if his condition worsens to the point of severely threatening his physical health.

column19: Your husband's symptoms of excessive thirst, frequent night-time urination, persistent fatigue, and blurred vision strongly suggest he has developed Diabetes Mellitus. High blood sugar prevents his cells from absorbing glucose for energy, which causes the fatigue, and it also alters the fluid levels in his eye lenses, resulting in blurry vision. He absolutely needs an urgent hospital visit to undergo a fasting blood glucose test, an HbA1c test, and a urinalysis to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other potential kidney issues. Immediately, he should avoid all sugary drinks, sweets, and refined carbohydrates, and instead eat more vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains. Once a doctor confirms the diagnosis and prescribes treatment, he will be advised on a schedule for regular blood sugar monitoring to ensure his condition is properly managed.

column19: In a fully immunized 3-year-old with no seizure history, the primary differential diagnoses for failing to respond to verbal cues or his name are severe hearing impairment and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). In our Nigerian context, sensorineural hearing loss is often secondary to severe neonatal jaundice or congenital infections, while conductive loss frequently stems from chronic otitis media. Conversely, ASD classically presents with impaired social reciprocity, poor eye contact, and unresponsiveness to name-calling despite intact auditory pathways. The critical next step in our clinic is to conduct a thorough otoscopic examination and arrange for objective audiological testing, such as Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) or Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA). If the audiological evaluation confirms normal hearing, a formal neurodevelopmental assessment is mandatory to diagnose ASD and facilitate early behavioral therapy.

This baby needs urgent full assessment first: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, chest indrawing, fever, ability to breastfeed, hydration, and chest examination, because this may be pneumonia, bronchiolitis, pertussis, aspiration, or another serious infection.
For IMCI practice, fast breathing in a 2–12 month old is ≥50 breaths/minute, and severe chest indrawing, inability to feed, cyanosis, or low oxygen are danger signs requiring urgent treatment/admission.

Management may include oxygen, suction, antibiotics if pneumonia is suspected, nebulization only if wheeze/bronchospasm is present, and other treatment based on examination findings.

This is most likely a **febrile convulsion**—a seizure triggered by high fever in a young child—but in Nigeria it is important to urgently check for causes such as **malaria, meningitis, pneumonia, or sepsis**.
During the seizure, lay the child on the **side**, protect the head, loosen tight clothes, and **do not put anything in the mouth** or try to force-feed.
If the seizure lasts more than **5 minutes**, or the child remains unconscious, rush to the nearest hospital; health workers may give **rectal diazepam or buccal/intranasal midazolam** to stop the seizure.
Reduce fever with **paracetamol**, remove excess clothing, and continue breastfeeding when fully awake.
The child should be assessed urgently with temperature check, malaria test, blood sugar, and examination for meningitis or other serious infection, then treated according to the cause.

Neonates possess poorly developed thermoregulation; thus, severe systemic infections and a lack of caloric intake to generate metabolic heat cause them to become extremely cold rather than feverish. While inadequate breastfeeding accelerates this rapid clinical decline, an overwhelming systemic bacterial infection is the primary underlying cause of the coldness and absent reflexes. This is a neonatal emergency requiring immediate admission for active rewarming, intravenous glucose administration, and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics to save the baby's life. The scheduled immunizations must be strictly deferred, as vaccinating a critically ill neonate is medically contraindicated until the life-threatening infection is treated and the baby is fully stable.

Bluish or dark lips in a newborn during breastfeeding usually means low oxygen in the blood (cyanosis), and difficulty breathing or suddenly stopping feeds is a serious danger sign requiring immediate hospital care.
Possible causes include congenital heart disease, pneumonia/sepsis, choking or aspiration during feeding, airway problems, prematurity-related breathing problems, low blood sugar, or seizures; liver disease usually causes yellow eyes/skin rather than blue lips and breathing distress.
Other danger signs are fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, flaring nostrils, poor feeding, limpness, abnormal sleepiness, fever or low temperature, convulsions, repeated vomiting, jaundice in the first 24 hours, or fewer wet nappies.
At home, do not give medicines: stop feeding, keep the baby warm, place her on her side or upright, gently clear visible milk/mucus from the nose/mouth, and go to the emergency unit immediately.
In hospital the baby may need oxygen, suction, blood sugar correction, antibiotics if infection is suspected, and urgent assessment for heart disease or other neonatal emergencies.

column19: Severe lower abdominal pain and heavy vaginal bleeding during pregnancy are typically caused by life-threatening obstetric emergencies such as a miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or placental abruption. Key warning signs that a pregnancy is in jeopardy include unrelenting abdominal cramps, passing large blood clots or tissue, profound maternal weakness or fainting, and a sudden loss of fetal movement. Heavy bleeding days after delivery is an emergency called secondary postpartum haemorrhage, commonly caused by retained placenta/tissue, poor contraction of the womb, infection of the womb, untreated tears, or rarely a bleeding disorder.
She should be assessed urgently: check vital signs, examine the uterus and birth canal, do blood tests/cross-match, give IV fluids, and transfuse blood if she is very weak or anaemic.
Treatment may include uterotonics such as oxytocin or misoprostol, antibiotics if infection is suspected, tranexamic acid where appropriate, removal of retained tissue, and repair of any tears; iron and folic acid help rebuild her blood after bleeding is controlled.
Advise her not to manage this at home—return immediately if bleeding soaks pads, she feels dizzy/faints, has fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe abdominal pain, or worsening weakness.
The baby should continue breastfeeding if possible and be checked for weight, feeding, jaundice, cord infection, and immunizations, while the mother gets rest, nutritious food, fluids, and follow-up after treatment.

Yes, his withdrawal, sadness, poor appetite, and loss of interest after his mother’s death may be grief, but because it is affecting eating, talking, and play, he should be assessed for childhood depression or traumatic grief.
At home, keep a calm routine, stay close to him, encourage him gently to talk about his mother or express feelings through drawing/play, reassure him he is loved and not to blame, and involve trusted relatives, teachers, and age-mates without forcing or scolding him.
Offer small frequent meals and fluids, eat with him, praise small efforts, and gradually reintroduce enjoyable activities.
He should speak with a trained mental health professional such as a child psychologist, psychiatrist, counsellor, or mental health nurse for grief counselling and assessment.
Medicine is not usually the first treatment, but may be needed if a specialist diagnoses moderate/severe depression; seek urgent help if he talks about death, self-harm, refuses food or fluids, loses weight, or becomes confused or aggressive.

column19: Yes, the boy's symptoms of isolation, loss of appetite, and profound sadness are direct psychological responses to the traumatic loss of his mother, indicating severe childhood grief that may be developing into clinical depression. At home, you can help by providing a consistent, loving, and patient environment, encouraging him with small portions of his favorite foods without forcefully pressuring him to eat. It is highly recommended that he speaks with a child psychologist or mental health professional who can use age-appropriate counseling, such as play therapy, to help him process his trauma. Currently, psychotherapy and strong psychosocial support from the family are the primary and safest treatments for a child his age. Psychiatric medications are generally avoided in young children for grief unless counseling fails and his condition becomes life-threatening.

column19: Based on WHO Integrated Management of Childhood Illness guidelines standard in Nigeria, a severe cough with respiratory distress in a young child strongly indicates severe pneumonia caused by bacterial or viral pathogens. Breathing becomes labored because the lung alveoli fill with inflammatory fluid, impairing gas exchange and forcing the child to use accessory respiratory muscles. The caregiver must immediately take the child to a healthcare facility for urgent clinical assessment and oxygen saturation monitoring. Standard local treatment requires prompt administration of injectable antibiotics like ceftriaxone and supplemental oxygen therapy to correct hypoxemia. Preventing future episodes relies on ensuring the child receives routine immunizations, including the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and maintaining adequate nutrition.

column19: Your 5-month-old baby’s symptoms of a persistent cough, nasal congestion, and especially the recent onset of irregular, difficult breathing are critical danger signs that strongly suggest a severe lower respiratory tract infection, such as pneumonia or bronchiolitis. You must take the baby to the nearest clinic or hospital immediately for urgent clinical evaluation, as respiratory distress in infants can rapidly become life-threatening and often requires supplemental oxygen or targeted antibiotics. Please do not give the baby any over-the-counter cough syrups, as they are highly unsafe for infants and will not treat the underlying infection. To temporarily relieve the severe nasal blockage at home, you can apply normal saline nasal drops into the baby's nostrils to loosen the mucus. Continue to offer frequent breastfeeding and fluids to keep his immune system supported and maintain hydration, but prioritize getting him emergency medical care today.

Two weeks after delivery, light bleeding can be normal lochia, but passage of “fleshy” tissue, a feeling that something is coming out, worsening lower abdominal pain, or continued bleeding may suggest retained placental/membrane tissue, infection of the womb, poor uterine contraction, or rarely pelvic organ prolapse.
Lower abdominal pain is concerning if it is severe, worsening, associated with fever, foul-smelling discharge, heavy bleeding, dizziness, weakness, or pain when passing urine.
She should go urgently to a hospital or maternity clinic for examination, vital signs, blood tests, and pelvic ultrasound; treatment may include antibiotics, medicines to contract the womb, removal of retained tissue, and treatment of anaemia or bleeding.
Warning signs after childbirth include soaking more than one pad per hour, large clots or tissue, bad-smelling discharge, fever, fainting, severe headache/blurred vision, swollen painful leg, chest pain, wound discharge, or inability to pass urine.
To reduce risk, mothers should deliver with skilled attendants, ensure the placenta is checked after birth, attend postnatal visits, maintain genital hygiene, avoid inserting herbs or substances into the vagina, breastfeed if possible, take prescribed medicines/iron, and seek care early for any abnormal change.

column19: No, it is not appropriate to simply prescribe medication for home use; a complete and urgent physical examination of the infant must be performed immediately. A 6-month-old presenting with a prolonged two-week cough that has progressed to severe difficulty breathing and tachypnea exhibits classic red-flag signs of a critical lower respiratory tract infection, such as severe pneumonia or bronchiolitis. According to Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) guidelines widely used in community settings, an infant in respiratory distress requires urgent clinical assessment to determine the need for hospitalization, supplemental oxygen, and parenteral antibiotics. Furthermore, prescribing more cough syrup is contraindicated, as over-the-counter liquid cough medications are not recommended for infants due to the risk of dangerous side effects and lack of efficacy.

This newborn has multiple danger signs: refusal to feed, extreme lethargy, hypothermia, absent movement/reflexes, and cold limbs, which suggest a life-threatening condition such as severe neonatal sepsis/meningitis, hypoglycaemia, severe hypothermia, birth asphyxia, prematurity/low birth weight, or a metabolic problem.
The body may feel very cold because sick newborns cannot regulate temperature well, especially when they are infected, not feeding, hypoglycaemic, exposed to cold, or small/premature.
This is not caused by breastfeeding refusal alone; refusal to suck is often a sign of serious underlying illness.
The baby needs immediate admission and emergency care: check temperature and blood glucose, start warming, give oxygen if needed, give IV dextrose/fluids, take sepsis evaluation where possible, and start urgent antibiotics such as ampicillin plus gentamicin according to neonatal protocol.
Do not proceed with routine immunization today while the baby is critically ill; stabilize and treat first, then give the due vaccines as soon as the baby is clinically stable.

Poor feeding with easy tiredness, sweating during breastfeeding, and fast or laboured breathing is a danger sign and commonly suggests heart failure from congenital heart disease, though severe chest infection, sepsis, anemia, or other serious illness can also cause it.
Yes, the breathing pattern may indicate a serious health problem, especially if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, grunting, flaring nostrils, pauses in breathing, or bluish lips/tongue.
Parents should urgently seek care if the baby feeds poorly, becomes weak or unusually sleepy, has fever or low temperature, fewer wet diapers, poor weight gain, vomiting, convulsions, or any blue discoloration.
Sweating on the head/face during feeding happens because feeding is hard work for a sick baby, especially when the heart is struggling to pump enough blood; overheating or fever can contribute but do not explain laboured breathing.
The baby should be taken to hospital promptly for examination, oxygen level check, chest assessment, and likely tests such as echocardiography, chest X-ray, and blood tests.

column19: This pregnant woman is experiencing severe anxiety and stress-induced hypertension secondary to Intimate Partner Violence (IPV), which poses a critical medical threat to both maternal and fetal well-being. Her immediate priority must be physical safety; she should not return to the abusive home and must relocate to a safe environment with supportive family members or a local women's shelter to eliminate the primary trigger of her trauma. She must strictly avoid traditional herbal mixtures like "agbo," as they are ineffective for trauma-induced panic, remain unregulated, and can cause severe organ toxicity or miscarriage during pregnancy. Clinically, she requires urgent antenatal evaluation to rule out preeclampsia and may be prescribed pregnancy-safe antihypertensive medications, such as Methyldopa, to manage her dangerously elevated blood pressure. Finally, to restore her mental health and overcome her overwhelming fear, she should be referred to a hospital-based medical social worker or community psychiatric nurse for trauma counseling and continuous psychosocial support.

column19: The intense pain your daughter is experiencing is caused by strong uterine muscle contractions and the stretching of the cervix as it dilates to prepare for birth. It is entirely normal and expected for a first-time mother's labor to be significantly longer and often more difficult, as her body has never been through this physiological process before. While it is possible the baby is too large for her pelvis (a condition called cephalopelvic disproportion), the medical team is monitoring her cervical dilation closely to ensure labor is progressing safely. If the doctors determine that the labor is obstructed or if there is any distress to the mother or baby, they will promptly perform a Cesarean section, which is a standard, life-saving procedure in such situations. You made the best decision by bringing her to the hospital where skilled professionals can continuously assess her progress and intervene appropriately to ensure the safety of both your daughter and the baby.

While home care is supportive, these specific danger signs mandate immediate hospital treatment with oxygen and antibiotics like amoxicillin, as respiratory infections are a leading cause of infant mortality in our region. Additionally, keeping the infant slightly elevated, ensuring adequate room ventilation, and strictly avoiding indoor air pollutants like firewood smoke will significantly reduce airway irritation and ease nighttime breathing.

You must avoid massaging the abdomen, as rubbing the womb will irritate the delicate tissues and significantly worsen the hemorrhage. column19: A hard, painless breast lump can be caused by benign conditions like fibroadenomas and cysts, or more serious issues like breast cancer. Not every lump means cancer; in fact, the vast majority of breast lumps are completely benign, but a persistent, hard mass always requires a definitive medical evaluation. In our local African community clinics, late presentation of breast cancer is a severe challenge, so we rely on immediate clinical breast exams, ultrasounds, and biopsies to rule out malignancy early. Women must also pay close attention to other red-flag symptoms such as bloody nipple discharge, skin dimpling (resembling an orange peel), an inverted nipple, and swollen lymph nodes in the armpit. The patient made an excellent decision to seek professional care, as early diagnosis is the most effective way to manage breast abnormalities and ensure her long-term health.

This is a gynecological emergency: first assess airway/breathing/circulation, check vital signs, insert two large-bore IV lines, give normal saline/Ringer’s lactate, take blood for grouping/crossmatch, transfuse if unstable or severely anaemic, give oxygen, catheterize to monitor urine, and urgently involve a gynecologist.
Because her last period was about 6 weeks ago, do an urgent urine/serum pregnancy test; if positive, consider miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, or molar pregnancy, and manage with pelvic ultrasound, possible uterine evacuation for incomplete miscarriage, or urgent surgery if ectopic rupture is suspected.
To reduce bleeding while assessing her, appropriate hospital treatments may include tranexamic acid, high-dose progestin or combined hormonal therapy if not pregnant, iron therapy after stabilization, and pain control; misoprostol/oxytocin or manual vacuum aspiration may be used only when miscarriage or retained products are confirmed.
Key tests include full blood count, blood group/Rh and crossmatch, pregnancy test/β-hCG, pelvic ultrasound, clotting profile, renal/liver function tests, and speculum/bimanual examination to look for cervical lesions, infection, fibroids, polyps, or trauma.
After stabilization, recurrent heavy painful bleeding should be investigated for fibroids, adenomyosis, endometrial problems, bleeding disorders, hormonal causes, and infection, with referral for definitive treatment.

Women must also monitor for other critical warning signs such as nipple retraction, bloody discharge, skin dimpling resembling an orange peel, and swollen armpit lymph nodes. Promoting routine breast self-awareness and early clinical presentation is crucial in our region to ensure timely intervention and improve overall survival outcomes.

column19: This pregnant woman is experiencing severe anxiety and stress-induced hypertension secondary to Intimate Partner Violence (IPV), which poses a critical medical threat to both maternal and fetal well-being. Her immediate priority must be physical safety; she should not return to the abusive home and must relocate to a safe environment with supportive family members or a local women's shelter to eliminate the primary trigger of her trauma. She must strictly avoid traditional herbal mixtures like "agbo," as they are ineffective for trauma-induced panic, remain unregulated, and can cause severe organ toxicity or miscarriage during pregnancy. Clinically, she requires urgent antenatal evaluation to rule out preeclampsia and may be prescribed pregnancy-safe antihypertensive medications, such as Methyldopa, to manage her dangerously elevated blood pressure. Finally, to restore her mental health and overcome her overwhelming fear, she should be referred to a hospital-based medical social worker or community psychiatric nurse for trauma counseling and continuous psychosocial support.

The commonest and most important cause to exclude is hearing impairment, which may be congenital or due to recurrent ear infections, chronic otitis media with fluid, impacted wax, measles/meningitis in the past, jaundice at birth, prematurity, birth asphyxia, or exposure to ototoxic drugs.
Another major possibility is autism spectrum disorder, especially if the child also has poor eye contact, does not point or share interest, prefers playing alone, has repetitive behaviours, or delayed speech.
Other causes include global developmental delay/intellectual disability, severe speech-language delay, psychosocial neglect or very low stimulation at home, and rarely visual impairment or other neurological problems even without seizures.
Being fully immunized and having no history of seizures is reassuring, but it does not rule out deafness, autism, or developmental delay.
This child should have ear examination, formal hearing assessment such as OAE/ABR or audiology referral, and developmental assessment as soon as possible, because early intervention improves outcomes.

column19: This severe, paroxysmal cough causing respiratory distress strongly suggests Pertussis (whooping cough), severe pneumonia, or possibly foreign body aspiration, which are conditions frequently encountered in our communities. Diagnostic evaluation in our setting should include a thorough clinical examination, pulse oximetry, a complete blood count to look for marked lymphocytosis typical of pertussis, and a chest X-ray to evaluate for lung consolidation. Treatment involves immediate supportive care such as oxygen therapy to ease breathing, alongside a course of macrolide antibiotics like Azithromycin to eradicate the underlying bacterial infection and reduce contagiousness. The caregiver must be advised to temporarily isolate the child to prevent spreading this highly contagious disease to other children and to keep the child calm to avoid triggering further coughing spasms. Furthermore, it is crucial to counsel the caregiver on the vital importance of strictly adhering to the routine childhood immunization schedule, particularly completing the Pentavalent vaccine series, to prevent future life-threatening infections.

A severe cough with night-time breathlessness and a whistling sound in the chest is commonly due to asthma or recurrent wheeze, but pneumonia, bronchiolitis, whooping cough, tuberculosis, or a foreign body in the airway must also be considered.
Night symptoms happen because the airways become narrow and inflamed, often triggered by cold air, viral infections, dust, smoke, perfumes, mosquito coils, animal dander, mould, or exercise.
Danger signs needing urgent hospital care include fast breathing, chest indrawing, inability to talk/cry/feed, bluish lips, severe weakness or drowsiness, persistent high fever, noisy breathing at rest, convulsions, or worsening despite inhaler treatment.
To reduce attacks, avoid cigarette smoke, cooking smoke, dust, strong smells, aerosol sprays, mosquito coils, cold exposure, and giving cough mixtures or antibiotics without a clinician’s advice.
The child should be assessed by a health worker for oxygen level, chest examination, and treatment such as inhaled salbutamol with a spacer, and possibly steroids or antibiotics if indicated.

column19: A newborn's lips changing color indicates cyanosis, a dangerous sign of low oxygen in the blood, which, along with breathing difficulty during feeding, strongly suggests a serious underlying condition like congenital heart disease or a severe respiratory infection, rather than liver disease. Difficulty breathing while feeding is a critical neonatal danger sign because the exertion of sucking unmasks underlying cardiopulmonary compromise that cannot meet the body's oxygen demands. Other critical danger signs parents must watch for include fever or hypothermia, inability to feed at all, extreme lethargy, convulsions, and severe chest indrawing. In a community setting, immediate emergency management consists of keeping the baby warm, ensuring the airway is clear by slightly extending the neck, withholding oral feeds to prevent aspiration, and immediately transporting the infant to a hospital for oxygen therapy and urgent medical evaluation.

column19: Based on the persistent cough, nocturnal breathing difficulty, and negative TB test, the most likely diagnosis is bronchial asthma, a common condition where airway inflammation causes night-time bronchospasms. In a five-year-old, nocturnal dyspnea and chronic cough occur because natural circadian drops in anti-inflammatory hormones like cortisol lead to increased airway hyperreactivity while sleeping. In our community setting, we must also evaluate for adenoid hypertrophy or allergic rhinitis, which can cause post-nasal drip and mimic these exact night-time respiratory symptoms. Please stop the unprescribed syrup and bring the child to the clinic for a physical examination and a therapeutic trial of inhaled salbutamol and corticosteroids. These evidence-based inhalers are locally available, highly effective for pediatric asthma, and will directly relieve the underlying airway constriction causing his night-time distress.

column19: The passage of flesh-like tissue, abnormal bleeding, and lower abdominal pain two weeks postpartum strongly indicates Retained Products of Conception (RPOC) likely complicated by a pelvic infection like endometritis. While mild cramping is normal during uterine involution, worsening lower abdominal pain or systemic aches are critical warning signs of retained placental fragments or developing sepsis. New mothers must vigilantly monitor for red-flag symptoms such as fever, foul-smelling lochia, heavy bleeding, and severe pelvic pain. She requires immediate medical evaluation at a healthcare facility for a pelvic ultrasound and clinical examination to confirm the diagnosis. Standard management in our community hospitals involves prompt uterine evacuation, often using manual vacuum aspiration, alongside broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent life-threatening secondary hemorrhage and sepsis.

In our local setting, this combination of symptoms is a medical emergency often caused by severe *Plasmodium falciparum* malaria destroying red blood cells or a severe viral infection acutely affecting the liver. Your siblings require immediate hospital admission for intravenous fluids to treat severe dehydration and urgent laboratory tests to confirm the exact diagnosis. Once diagnosed, we will immediately initiate life-saving treatments, such as intravenous Artesunate if it is severe malaria, alongside aggressive supportive care. Please stop all home remedies immediately, as they can cause further liver toxicity, and allow our medical team to begin this emergency management right away.

column19: While paracetamol and oral hydration are appropriate supportive measures, you must initiate an Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) immediately rather than delaying it, as Nigerian guidelines mandate prompt treatment for confirmed malaria in postpartum women. Delaying antimalarials in a weak, symptomatic patient risks progression to severe malaria; therefore, start oral artemether-lumefantrine now since she can tolerate oral fluids. Continue encouraging exclusive breastfeeding, as the newborn's stooling is a normal physiological response, but closely monitor the mother for signs of puerperal sepsis like uterine tenderness or foul-smelling lochia that would require antibiotics. Reassess her clinical status within 24 hours to ensure symptomatic improvement and adherence to the full ACT course. Urgently refer her to a higher-level facility for intravenous artesunate if she develops danger signs such as persistent vomiting, inability to drink, or altered consciousness.

column19: The newborn's lethargy and poor cry, despite normal breathing and temperature, are most likely due to mild birth asphyxia, neonatal hypoglycemia, or the lingering effects of pain medications administered to the mother during labor. Rather than immediate medication, the infant requires gentle tactile stimulation, close monitoring, a blood glucose check, and early initiation of breastfeeding to stabilize energy levels. Once discharged, the mother must practice exclusive breastfeeding on demand and strictly avoid giving the baby water, formula, or traditional herbal mixtures, which can cause severe infections and malnutrition. To support optimal recovery and abundant breast milk production, the mother should consume a balanced, locally available diet rich in proteins, iron, and fluids, such as beans, fish, and dark green leafy vegetables.

column19: Your husband's symptoms strongly suggest allergic asthma and rhinitis, which occur because his immune system hyper-reacts to environmental triggers like dust and cooking smoke rather than just the dust itself. To confirm this, we can perform a Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) test or spirometry to assess his lung function and airway reversibility, which are standard, accessible diagnostic tools in our community hospitals. For effective management, he requires a salbutamol reliever inhaler for acute breathlessness, a daily inhaled corticosteroid to reduce underlying airway inflammation, and oral antihistamines to control the sneezing. Consistent use of these medications alongside practical trigger avoidance, such as wearing a face mask in dusty areas and improving kitchen ventilation, will stabilize his hyper-reactive airways and allow him to breathe comfortably anywhere.

Dog bites can cause serious bacterial wound infection and rabies; rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start, so start post-exposure treatment immediately.
Wash the wound under running water with soap for at least 15 minutes, apply iodine/chlorhexidine, avoid herbs or tight dressings, and do not close the wound unless a clinician decides it is safe.
Because the dog is unvaccinated and the bite broke the skin, give rabies vaccine today on days 0, 3, 7, and 14, plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound if it is a deep/transdermal bite or saliva contacted broken skin.
Also give tetanus vaccination/immune globulin depending on the child’s tetanus history, antibiotics such as amoxicillin-clavulanate for 5–7 days, and pain relief; admit or use IV antibiotics if fever, spreading redness, pus, or severe swelling develops.
The dog should be confined and observed by veterinary/public health officers for 10 days, while the child’s wound may need surgical cleaning, culture if pus is present, and X-ray if the bite is deep, near a joint/bone, or a tooth fragment is suspected.

column19: A severe cough with difficulty breathing and wheezing, particularly worsening at night, strongly suggests childhood asthma, though lower respiratory infections like pneumonia can also cause these symptoms. Crucial danger signs to look out for include abnormally fast breathing, deep lower chest wall indrawing, bluish discoloration of the lips, stridor at rest, and an inability to drink or breastfeed. These danger signs indicate severe respiratory distress or hypoxia, requiring immediate emergency medical treatment to prevent life-threatening complications. To manage and reduce the frequency of such episodes, it is highly recommended to protect the child from common environmental triggers like indoor cooking smoke, cigarette smoke, excessive dust, strong odors, and cold air. A child with severe cough that stops breathing may have pneumonia, pertussis/whooping cough, asthma or bronchiolitis, croup, tuberculosis, or inhalation of a foreign body; this is a danger sign and needs urgent hospital assessment.
Tests may include oxygen saturation, temperature/respiratory rate, chest examination, chest X-ray, full blood count, malaria test where relevant, sputum or gastric aspirate/GeneXpert for TB if suspected, and nasopharyngeal swab for pertussis/viral infection if available.
Treatment depends on the cause but may include oxygen, nebulized salbutamol if wheezing, antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia or azithromycin for suspected pertussis, steroids for croup/asthma, and urgent bronchoscopy if a foreign body is suspected.
The caregiver should take the child to a health facility immediately, keep the child sitting upright, avoid smoke/dust, continue feeding/fluids if safe, and not give cough suppressants or herbal mixtures.
They should return urgently if there is fast breathing, chest indrawing, blue lips, inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, or worsening breathing, and ensure routine immunizations including pentavalent/pertussis and measles vaccines are up to date.

A 7-day-old baby who is not breastfeeding well and has noisy or difficult breathing should be taken to a hospital or emergency paediatric unit today, because poor feeding in a newborn can be a sign of serious illness such as neonatal infection/sepsis, pneumonia, low blood sugar, dehydration, or significant nasal blockage.
Newborns breathe mainly through the nose, so even simple nasal congestion can make them pull off the breast repeatedly, but the same symptoms can also occur with infection or breathing problems that need examination and possibly oxygen, antibiotics, or fluids.
It is less likely to be “water entering the head” during delivery if the baby was well before discharge, but problems can develop after going home.
While going to the hospital, keep the baby warm, try a few drops of normal saline in the nostrils and gently clear mucus, and offer expressed breast milk in small amounts if the baby can swallow safely.
Do not give herbal mixtures or over-the-counter cold medicines to a newborn.

column19: These symptoms—specifically the constant severe abdominal and back pain combined with vaginal bleeding and fluid leakage at six months—strongly indicate a life-threatening obstetric emergency like placental abruption or preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), rather than uncomplicated preterm labor or a simple miscarriage. Unlike typical preterm labor which features intermittent cramping, constant severe pain with bleeding is a hallmark clinical sign of placental abruption, risking severe maternal hemorrhage and fetal compromise. You must advise immediate emergency referral to a comprehensive obstetric facility for maternal stabilization, intravenous fluid resuscitation, and blood cross-matching, which are critical first steps in our resource-limited community settings. While an urgent ultrasound is useful to assess fetal viability and rule out placenta previa, it should never delay emergency clinical intervention because ultrasound has notoriously low sensitivity for detecting placental abruption. Therefore, treat this as an acute emergency where rapid clinical diagnosis and maternal resuscitation take precedence over imaging to prevent maternal and perinatal mortality.

column19: A newborn's lips turning blue (cyanosis) and experiencing breathing difficulty during breastfeeding are critical danger signs highly suggestive of congenital heart disease or severe respiratory illness, rather than liver disease, because feeding increases metabolic oxygen demand that a compromised cardiopulmonary system cannot meet. This is primary postpartum haemorrhage, an emergency; common causes are the “4 Ts”: uterine atony (womb not contracting—most common), trauma (cervical/vaginal/perineal tear or uterine rupture), tissue retained in the uterus (placenta/membranes or rarely an undelivered second twin), and thrombin problems (clotting disorder/DIC).
Call for help immediately, assess ABCs, give oxygen, insert two wide-bore IV lines, take blood for Hb/grouping/crossmatch/clotting, start rapid IV fluids and arrange blood transfusion while monitoring pulse, BP, urine output, and amount of bleeding.
Massage the uterus firmly, empty the bladder with a catheter, give oxytocin 10 IU IM or slow IV then 20–40 IU in 1 L IV fluid; if bleeding continues add misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual/rectal, tranexamic acid 1 g IV as soon as possible (repeat once after 30 minutes if needed), and ergometrine 0.2 mg IM/IV only if no hypertension or heart disease.
Check the placenta is complete and examine the birth canal with good light: remove retained tissue/placenta manually if needed with antibiotics, and suture cervical or vaginal tears promptly.
If bleeding does not stop quickly, do bimanual uterine compression and insert a uterine balloon/condom catheter tamponade if available, then urgently refer/transfer to a higher centre for surgery while continuing resuscitation and uterotonics.

column19: Based on the symptoms described, the newborn is most likely suffering from birth asphyxia, a critical condition where the baby's brain and organs do not receive enough oxygen before, during, or immediately after birth, leading to a weak cry, abnormal muscle tone, and poor feeding. Immediate emergency intervention should follow the "Helping Babies Breathe" protocol, which involves thoroughly drying and stimulating the baby, clearing the airway if obstructed, and urgently initiating positive pressure ventilation (bag-and-mask) to assist breathing. Additionally, blood samples should be taken for a complete blood count (CBC) and blood culture to rule out early-onset neonatal sepsis. While these interventions are ongoing, it is crucial to keep the baby warm to prevent hypothermia and prepare for intravenous fluid support or transfer to a specialized neonatal unit if the baby's condition does not rapidly improve.

column19: The bluish discoloration of the newborn's lips (cyanosis) and the struggle to breathe while breastfeeding strongly indicate a critical lack of oxygen in the blood. These are hallmark signs of an underlying congenital heart defect, where the heart cannot effectively pump oxygenated blood, or a severe respiratory infection such as neonatal pneumonia. Breastfeeding acts as a stress test for infants, and gasping for air reveals that the baby's cardiopulmonary system is failing to meet the body's increased oxygen demands during feeding. Therefore, medication should never be given blindly in this scenario; the baby requires an immediate and comprehensive medical investigation. Urgent clinical evaluation, including oxygen saturation monitoring and likely an echocardiogram or chest X-ray, is essential to establish an accurate diagnosis and initiate life-saving treatment.

During the seizure, lay the child on the **side**, protect the head, loosen tight clothes, and **do not put anything in the mouth** or try to force-feed.
If the seizure lasts more than **5 minutes**, or the child remains unconscious, rush to the nearest hospital; health workers may give **rectal diazepam or buccal/intranasal midazolam** to stop the seizure.
Reduce fever with **paracetamol**, remove excess clothing, and continue breastfeeding when fully awake.
The child should be assessed urgently with temperature check, malaria test, blood sugar, and examination for meningitis or other serious infection, then treated according to the cause.

column19: Aun, wetin dem fit carry pikin come hospital, e be possible pikin dey have condition called "autism spectrum disorder" (ASD). Pikin dem no dey respond to talk, no dey hear, na sign of ASD. Pikin no dey get seizure, na good, but still, ASD fit make pikin no dey respond like this. Pikin dem collect all vaccine, na good, but ASD still fit make pikin no dey respond. Dem fit take pikin for more test to confirm ASD and get proper treatment.

column19:
Serious cough wey dey worse for night plus chest sound/wheezing and hard breathing fit be asthma/“reactive airway”, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, croup/whooping cough, allergy, or something wey enter airway—so make dem carry pikin go hospital quick for check.
Danger signs na: fast breathing, chest dey draw in, nose dey flare, pikin no fit talk/cry/feed well, blue lips, very weak/sleepy, high fever, convulsion, noisy breathing even when e no dey cry, vomiting everything, or cough pass 2 weeks/blood for sputum.

Avoid smoke from firewood/kerosene/cigarette, dust, strong perfume/insecticide, cold air, overcrowding, and self-medication with antibiotics or cough syrup—especially for small pikin.
If breathing dey hard or chest dey “work” as you talk, no wait till morning; na emergency.

After delivery, we do all the necessary care for both the mama and the baby. Later, we carry both of them go one room make dem rest.

After some time, the woman call us come say her body dey very weak, she dey tire well well, and her eye dey somehow as if she no dey see clear. She still try chop after she born, but she find am hard to swallow the food. She continue to dey weak and she come dey feel dizzy too.

Wetin fit don happen? E fit be say she lose plenty blood during the delivery and now she need blood transfusion? Abi wetin suppose make we do for am? Should we give am food make she chop?
column19: Dis woman get postpartum hemorrhage wey don cause severe anemia, dat na why she weak, no fit see well, and no fit swallow food. You must check her PCV sharp sharp and crossmatch blood for urgent transfusion, because food no go solve dis kain blood loss. Put two big IV lines, give IV fluids like Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate fast fast, and monitor her vital signs every 15 minutes. Check if placenta complete and uterus dey contracted well, if not, massage uterus and give oxytocin or misoprostol to stop further bleeding. Refer am go higher center if blood no dey or she no dey improve, because dis na emergency wey fit kill am.

column19: Many things fit cause this kind strong lump for breast, like water-bag (cyst), infection, non-cancer tumor wey common well-well wey we dey call Fibroadenoma, and sometimes, breast cancer. The best step now na make she go hospital run breast scan (ultrasound) so that doctor go fit check am properly and her mind go rest.

column18:

column19: Mama, the baby need make he see doctor sharp-sharp because blue lip and gasping show say di baby no dey get enough oxygen. This fit be because of "Cyanotic Heart Disease" or some blockage for di baby heart/veins wey dey stop blood from reaching lungs. Sometimes, if di baby get "tracheomalacia" (soft windpipe), e go struggle to breathe especially when e dey suck breast. No try give any medicine for house because this one need expert check-up and maybe surgery to fix di problem. Carry di baby go hospital now make doctor check di heart and lungs sharp-sharp.

column18:
One woman dem carry come hospital this morning because she dey bleed plenty, and the bleeding don make her weak well-well. Dem ask am whether this kind thing don happen before, and she talk say e don happen about two times before. Anytime e happen, she dey feel pain and the bleeding dey come and stop, then come start again.

Dem come ask am whether e fit be say belle dey comot, but she talk say she no know whether she get belle or not. Dem ask am when she last see her monthly period, and she talk say not too long, say na about one month and two weeks ago she last see her period before this heavy bleeding start again this morning.

Abeg, wetin fit make dis woman bleed this kind plenty? Wetin be the emergency things wey health workers suppose do immediately? Wetin be the treatment wey fit save her life and stop the bleeding? Which medicine or injection wey fit help control the bleeding fit be given first? And which tests or investigations fit be done to know the real cause of this serious bleeding?
column19: Dis woman fit get incomplete abortion or ectopic pregnancy wey don burst, because she miss period for six weeks, get heavy bleeding with pain wey dey come and go, and don happen before. Health workers suppose check ABC immediately, put two big IV lines (16G or 18G), give Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate fast fast, crossmatch 4 units blood, and monitor vital signs every 15 minutes. Oxytocin 10 units IV stat or 20 units for 500ml drip na first medicine to contract uterus and reduce bleeding, Ergometrine 0.5mg IM fit add if BP normal. Do urgent pregnancy test (beta-hCG), PCV, grouping and crossmatching, clotting profile, and pelvic scan to confirm diagnosis and rule out ectopic. If products of conception dey inside, manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) or D&C na definitive treatment to stop bleeding and save her life.

column18:

column19: Pikin na likely na case of bronchiolitis or pneumonia. Wetin fit make pikin cough serious na bacteria or virus, like RSV or influenza. Danger sign wey fit watch out for include fever, wheezing, and rapid breathing. Woman should avoid smoke, dust, and strong smells. She fit give pikin fluids and monitor temperature. If pikin no fit breathe well, she fit take him to hospital for oxygen and antibiotics.

column18: One old papa come our local hospital The papa talk say he get serious headache Him neck dey stiff and rash don suddenly come out for him body He come ask wetin fit dey cause am and wetin be the correct treatment We ask am whether the headache start suddenly or e dey come small small The papa say e start suddenly for night and know Now e don become very severe We still ask am whether e fit look light well and e say no because light dey make di headache worse We ask am about di rash wey dey im body whether e dey pain am whether e plenty or e just small The papa say di rash dey all over im body e no fit point one place and e dey He itch am After that we ask whether he don contact with anybody wey sick recently The papa say dem no go any way apart from where dem dey sell go for front of the house and dem no know anybody wey sick wey dem don get contact with Our question for dr be wetin fit cause this kind serious headache and stiff neck wey make person no fit turn him neck plus rash all over the body Wetin fit be the cause Na infectious disease or na another sickness Our 2nd question be which kind test this papa suppose do to know exactly wetin dey worry am make e fit get correct treatment and which medicine dem fit start give am Before the test results go come out

column18: One woman been born pikin pikin like 5 months wey don pass She con explain say when she born the pikin nothing be de worry the pikin As the pikin been de chop plenty well well as them been expect Na just like that o see say the pikin go de Cry well well as something dey pain am for his leg and hin hands E been also con reach point wey the pikin go call person to con help am stand up to dey waka for ground or to dey move so that him go go where im mama dey Abeg wetin this woman fit do for the pikin so that But the thing wey dey pain the pikin for his hand and his leg go stop and wetin go fit make sure say this thing no go delay the way wey the pikin de grow So the mama wan come hospital with the pikin con seek dr to find out wetin dem fit do wey go help the pikin body dey better and make im health sef better
column19:
Make I try help you understand wetin fit dey happen.

For pikin wey be like 5 months wey dey cry well well when leg and hand dey pain am, and now e no fit stand or waka well, this fit be sign say the pikin get problem wit bone or blood - one big one na **sickle cell disease**, because e common well well for our area and e dey cause pain crisis for hand and leg (wetin dem dey call *hand-foot syndrome*).

The most important thing wey the mama fit do na to **carry the pikin come hospital make dem do blood test** (like Genotype test and Full Blood Count) so that dr go sabi if na sickle cell or if na something like bone infection, injury, or lack of blood (anaemia).

If dem confirm say na sickle cell, dr go start the pikin on medicine like **folic acid, penicillin prophylaxis, and vaccine** to prevent infection, and dem go teach the mama how to manage the pain crisis - all this go help make sure say the pikin go dey grow well without too much delay.

Wetin be di signs wey show say pregnancy dey for trouble? And e get any medicine wey fit stop di pain and bleeding without harming di baby wey dey for belle?
column19: Aye, when a woman get serious pain in belly and heavy bleeding during pregnancy, it be danger sign. This can be due to conditions like ectopic pregnancy, placental abruption, or preterm labor. Immediate medical attention is needed. At hospital, doctors can do tests like ultrasound, blood tests, and sometimes emergency surgery to save both mother and baby. Medicine like misoprostol can help stop bleeding but must be used carefully by doctors. Always seek medical help if you see these signs.

column18: One of my senior sibling just born baby girl few days ago as she dey give di pikin breast she come notice say anytime pikin dey suck breast e dey hard am to breathe Sometimes as di pikin dey suck but just stop sudden like say life no dey di body One midnight as di him mama dey breastfeed di pikin she come notice say di The pikin lips dey change color small small Fear catch am well well and she no know wetin to do She quickly carry di pikin upright make e fit breathe better But the pikin still dey struggle to breathe The papa too fear as e see say di pikin dey find am hard to breathe and di lips dey change color Dem no waste timeall Dem quickly carry the pikin go up I go hospital make doctors attend to am Wetin fit make new born pikin lips dey change color Abi difficulty to breathe why the pikin dey suck breast and dangerous sign How disease or liver disease fit make pikin dey struggle to breathe which other dangerous signs and symptoms wey pain I suppose dey watch out for And wetin be the emergency 1st treatment wey person fit give pikin wey dey struggle to breathe after medical help reach
column19: Di blue color for lips and breathing problem as pikin dey suck breast na very dangerous sign (cyanosis) wey mean say oxygen no reach di pikin body well, and e dey mostly happen because of congenital heart problem (like hole in the heart) or severe lung infection.
